profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-09T11:23:36.652+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: The fifth year of Chéng Hé.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month, at noon.
The first and fourth ships.
The envoys sailed the ships.
Due to a lack of favorable winds,
they anchored for three days.
On the seventeenth day, at midnight,
they caught a mountain breeze, hoisted the sails, and rowed onward.
At the hour of Sì, they reached the eastern sea of Zhìhè Island.
As there was no trustworthy wind,
they anchored for five days.
On the twenty-second day, at the hour of Mǎo,
they caught a northeast wind and set sail.
Without seeking a bay,
they sailed through the dark night.
On the twenty-third day, at the hour of Sì,
they arrived at Yǒujiù Island.
A northeast wind blew,
and they lingered, reluctant to part.
By the hour of Yǒu,
they hoisted the sails and crossed the sea.
The northeast wind blew,
and they sailed through the dark night.
The two ships exchanged fire signals.
On the twenty-fourth day, they saw the fourth ship ahead in the distance.
Between it and the first ship,
there was a distance of about thirty lǐ.
They sailed far to the west.
The chief envoy began to paint an image of Guānyīn Bodhisattva.
The invited scholar-monks and others
together recited scriptures and made vows and prayers.
At the hour of Hài, fire signals were exchanged.
Their appearance was like stars.
By dawn, they were no longer visible.
Although the winds shifted between northeast and southeast,
there was no fear of drifting off course.
Large bamboo, reed roots, cuttlefish, shellfish, and the like
flowed with the waves.
They lowered hooks to retrieve and examine them.
Some were alive, some withered.
The sea was light green,
and everyone said they were near land.
At the hour of Shēn, a large fish swam alongside the ship.
On the twenty-seventh day, the iron ballast was all washed away by the waves.
The exhausted birds lingered for two nights without leaving.
Sometimes they flew west two or three times,
then returned to their perch.
This happened repeatedly.
The sea was white-green.
All night, men were sent up the mast
to look for mountains or islands, but none were seen.
On the twenty-eighth day, early in the morning,
two egrets flew northwest.
The wind remained unchanged.
They turned the sails to the southwest.
At the hour of Sì, they reached white water.
Its color was like yellow mud.
Everyone said,
"This must be the great river flow of Yángzhōu."
They sent a man up the mast to look, and he reported:
"From the northwest, it flows straight south.
It is over twenty lǐ wide.
Looking ahead, the water ahead is light green again."
They sailed briefly,
and it turned out just as reported.
The chief envoy was deeply puzzled that the sea had turned light green again.
The Silla interpreter, Jīn Zhèngnán, reported:
"I have heard that the Juégǎng of Yángzhōu is difficult to pass.
Now that we have crossed the white water,
I suspect we have crossed Juégǎng."
At the hour of Wèi, the seawater also turned white.
Everyone was astonished.
They sent a man up the mast
to look for land or islands,
but he still reported seeing none.
The wind remained unchanged.
The sea was shallow, the waves high,
crashing like thunder.
They tied a rope to iron and lowered it,
reaching only five zhàng.
After a short while, they lowered iron to test the sea's depth,
and it was only five xún.
The envoys were afraid.
Some said,
"We should drop anchor and stop,
and proceed tomorrow."
Others said,
"We must lower half the sails and send out a boat
to learn the depth ahead,
then proceed gradually."
The proposal to stop
seemed inappropriate.
While they were debating,
it was almost the hours of Yǒu and Xū.
Then an east wind blew fiercely,
the waves grew high and violent,
and the ship suddenly rushed onto a sandbar.
In panic, they lowered the sails.
The rudder broke twice.
Waves from east and west crashed against the ship, tilting it.
The rudder blade struck the seabed.
The ship was about to break apart.
So they cut the mast and abandoned the rudder.
The ship then drifted with the waves.
When waves came from the east, the ship tilted west;
when waves came from the west, it tilted east.
Water washed over the deck,
beyond measure.
Everyone on board relied on the Buddha and gods,
all making vows and prayers.
Everyone was at a loss.
From the envoy leader down to the sailors,
they stripped naked, tightened their loincloths, and the ship was on the verge of breaking apart.
They ran back and forth from stern to bow,
each seeking a safe spot.
At the joints,
they were all loosened by the waves.
At the ends of the left and right railings,
they tied ropes and pulled,
struggling to find a way to survive. The bilge water overflowed,
and the ship settled into the sand.
Official and private belongings floated and sank in the bilge.
On the twenty-ninth day, at dawn, the tide ebbed,
and the bilge also dried up.
They sent men to inspect the bottom,
and it was completely cracked.
Sand buried the broken planks.
Everyone devised a plan:
"Now that the ship is cracked,
if the tide rises again,
I fear it will break apart further."
So they toppled the mast,
cut down the left and right stern railings, and erected oars around the ship.
They tied ropes to the broken planks.
At the hour of Hài, they saw
a distant firelight to the west.
Everyone faced it,
filled with joy.
They watched all night,
but no mountains or islands were seen,
only the firelight.
On the morning of the second day, the tide rose.
We chased after it for several hundred chō.
To the west, we saw an island that looked like two ships lying side by side.
In a short while, we proceeded.
Then we knew it was land.
We had not sailed far
when we encountered two opposing tidal currents.
We drifted sideways for about fifty chō.
The ship settled into the mud.
It could neither advance nor retreat.
Then the tide surged strongly,
scouring away the mud around the ship.
The mud churned up violently.
The ship suddenly capsized.
It was almost buried and sunk.
Everyone was terrified.
They vied to cling to the side of the ship.
Each wore only a loincloth.
Ropes were tied everywhere.
They tied themselves and waited for death.
Not long after,
the ship capsized to the left again.
The people moved to the right.
Wherever it capsized, they moved accordingly.
This happened several times in succession.
Also, the second layer of planking on the ship's bottom
broke off and drifted away.
Everyone was dispirited.
Weeping, they made vows.
At the hour of Xū and Hài (7-11 PM),
we saw something floating on the waves in the distance.
Everyone said,
"Could that be a ship coming to meet us?"
While we were doubting and discussing,
it came against the wind to meet us.
Finally, we knew it was indeed a boat.
We saw a small storage boat with people on board.
It was the one sent out the previous day,
carrying the archer Mibu no Kaizan
and six men from the Great Táng.
They hurried to the front of our ship.
The Roku-ji and those below him
first asked about the place where the Ambassador had landed.
The reply was:
"We do not know where he landed."
Hearing this, we were shocked and saddened.
Tears were hard to hold back.
Immediately, we transferred the national gifts and goods onto that boat.
One Roku-ji,
two officials in charge of the ship,
the study monk Enzai and twenty-seven others below him,
all transferred and boarded it together.
Pointing toward land, we set off.
At noon, we reached the river mouth.
In the afternoon, we arrived at Dōng Liángfēng Village, Sāngtián Township, Báicháo Town, Hǎilíng County, Yángzhōu.
It was the second day of the seventh month in the fifth year of Jōwa in Japan.
That is, the second day of the seventh month in the third year of Kāichéng in the Great Táng.
Although the era names differed,
the month and day were the same.
The study monks and others stayed overnight at the residence of Jì Bīn in the garrison of the Shǒuzhuō army.
We heard that the Ambassador, at the hour of Wèi (1-3 PM) on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month,
had left the ship.
Afterward, during the drifting,
the wind was strong and the waves fierce.
Fearing the ship would sink,
they cast anchor and threw things overboard.
Chanting the names of Guānyīn and Miàojiàn,
they prayed for a way to survive.
The fierce wind stopped at times.
At midnight, they drifted to the southern reed marshes by the great river mouth.
At dawn on the first day of the seventh month,
the tide ebbed, and they could not proceed.
They ordered someone to climb the masthead to look for mountains and villages.
Far to the south were three mountains.
They did not know their names.
The countryside was remote and secluded.
There was no one to ask.
If they waited for the tide to rise,
they feared it would take too long and night would fall,
making it impossible to rescue those on the ship.
So they tied ropes to the ship
and pulled it to the seaside.
The number of people was very few.
They could not move it.
The judges and those below them
took the cables and pulled.
In the afternoon, they launched a small boat
and traveled along the shore.
Gradually, they sought the river mouth.
Finally, they reached the great river mouth.
The tide was against them, and the current was swift.
They could not proceed.
The river was somewhat shallow.
The sailors and others went into the water and pulled the boat along.
It was difficult to find people.
By chance, they met a reed seller.
They immediately asked about the region and village.
He replied:
"This is the great river mouth of Huáinán Town, Hǎilíng County, Yángzhōu in the Great Táng."
They immediately summoned two of those merchants
to board the boat and head toward Huáinán Town.
Traveling by waterway, halfway there,
those two men did not know the town office.
They pointed back toward the river mouth and returned.
As night fell, they stayed at the river mouth.
On the evening of the second day, those two men left.
Nearby, there was a salt official.
They dispatched Judge Nagamine no Sukune Takana, following Roku-ji Takacka no Sukune Momo-oki,
ordering them to go to the town office.
Along with sending a written message, the salt official Judge Yuán Xíngcún
came by small boat to offer condolences.
The envoys wrote about the customs of their country.
The Ambassador also presented local products and again headed toward Huáinán Town.
Traveling north from the river mouth for about fifteen lǐ,
they arrived at the town office. The town soldiers and others reported, saying:
"You should return toward Juégǎngtíng."
Immediately, they took two town soldiers back to the river mouth.
As they were about to reach the river mouth,
Judge Yuán Xíngcún,
by the waterway, reported, saying:
"Today it is already late.
You should stay overnight."
Following his words, they stayed.
His kind inquiries were especially deep.
Moreover, he added a guide.
At the hour of Chǒu (1-3 AM) on the third day, the tide rose.
A boat that knew the way led ahead,
and they proceeded toward Juégǎngtíng.
At the hour of Sì (9-11 AM), they reached Báihúkǒu.
The current was extremely swift against them.
Three men from the Great Táng,
along with sailors from our country,
pulled the boat across the current.
They reached the shore and tied the cables.
They waited briefly for the tide to rise.
Here, they heard that the fourth ship had drifted and landed in the northern sea.
At noon, they barely arrived at Zhōng Village in the garrison of the Shǒuzhuō army under the jurisdiction of Báicháo Town, Hǎilíng County.
Here, Roku-ji Yamashiro no Uji Masu and over thirty others, who had parted earlier at sea, came out to meet them.
Meeting again, sorrow and joy mingled together.
Shedding tears, they expressed their feelings.
Here, the whole group stayed together.
During this time, they hired small boats and such
to transport the national gifts and goods,
and to wash and dry the official and private items damaged by moisture.
Although several days had passed,
there had been no consolation from the prefecture or county.
Each person sought lodging as best they could.
They suffered no little hardship.
The invited Dharma Master
stayed with the study monks in one place.
Eighteen lǐ from Dōng Liángfēng Village,
there was Yánhǎi Village.
In the village, there was a temple,
named Guóqīng Temple.
The Ambassador and others, to rest from the fatigue of drifting,
stayed here to lodge.
At the hour of Sì (9-11 AM) on the ninth day,
Liǔ Miǎn, the Commissioner of Hǎilíng Town, came to console the envoys and others.
He presented wine and cakes.
Moreover, he arranged music.
Eight officers, guards, and attendants accompanied him.
This Liǔ Miǎn wore purple court robes.
The village's Yā-guān
also similarly wore purple clothes.
After the inspection was completed,
they returned to the county office.
On the twelfth day, from Dōng Liángfēng Village, they took the waterway to transport their personal belongings.
They placed them in the temple, finishing the task.
On the same day at noon,
to hasten the arrival of the welcoming boats,
they dispatched the interpreter Ōyake no Toshio,
the archer Ōyake no Miyatsugu and others,
ordering them to go to the county office by waterway.
At the hour of Shēn (3-5 PM), it thundered.
The study monks and others were staying in Dōngfēng Village.
They had not yet come here.
On the thirteenth day, it was very hot.
At the hour of Wèi (1-3 PM), it thundered.
Since first drifting ashore,
mosquitoes and midges had been very numerous.
They were as large as flies.
At night, they tormented people.
The hardship was extreme.
At the hour of Shēn (3-5 PM), the study monks came.
They stayed together in the temple.
They suffered from dysentery.
At the hour of Chén (7-9 AM) on the fourteenth day,
because the welcoming boats from the county and prefecture had not come,
one Ambassador, two Judges, one Roku-ji, one official in charge of the ship, one scribe, archers, sailors, and others, thirty people in total,
went by waterway toward the county office.
At that time, monk Yuán Xù from Kāiyuán Temple came.
He communicated by writing.
He was quite knowledgeable in literature.
He inquired and learned about our country's customs.
Moreover, he presented local products.
That monk presented peaches and fruits.
Near the temple, there was his cloister.
After a brief conversation, he returned.
At dusk, it thundered and rained heavily.
The alarm and distress were especially severe.
On the seventeenth day, at noon, the archer, the chief officer, and more than ten others.
Departed from the Rúgāo garrison.
Bringing over thirty grass boats.
Immediately heard that the ambassador had arrived at the garrison yesterday.
At the shēn hour, the spring official, the mountain clerk, and others.
Came with the archer from Dōngliángfēng Village.
Stayed overnight at the temple.
On the eighteenth day, early morning.
Public and private goods were loaded onto the boats.
At the sì hour, the clerk and below, the sailors and above, went by waterway toward the prefecture.
Two water buffalo were used to pull over forty boats.
Some were grouped three vessels into one boat.
Some were grouped two vessels into one boat.
Tied together with ropes.
The journey ahead and behind was hard to hear.
Calling out to each other frequently.
The journey was swift.
The canal dug was over two zhàng wide.
Straight flowing without bends.
This was dug by Emperor Suí Yáng.
Rain fell, making it arduous.
Traveled over thirty lǐ.
At the shēn hour, arrived at Guōbǔ Village and stopped to stay.
Entering the night, many mosquitoes.
Painful like needle pricks.
Extremely difficult.
Drums were beaten all night.
It is the custom of this country.
There are guards.
To protect official goods, drums are beaten at night.
On the nineteenth day, at the yín hour.
The water buffalo pulled forward to set off.
Dark clouds but no rain.
At the mǎo hour, heard the rooster's crow.
Began to see Wú bamboo groves, raw millet, small horn beans, etc.
At the sì hour, the ambassador's dispatch arrived.
Arrived.
According to the dispatch document, it stated.
The damaged drifting ship.
Should be inspected as appropriate by the responsible officials.
The guarding and seizing office, its ship guards, sailors, etc., should be ordered to proceed upward according to the number.
Must not be detained.
Immediately dispatched the boat master Shǐ Hóu Sīwán and others.
To return to where the ship was anchored.
At noon, arrived at Línhécāng Post.
Traveled all night.
On the twentieth day, at mǎo hour, arrived at Chì'àn Village.
Asked the locals.
They replied.
From here, travel one hundred twenty lǐ.
There is the Rúgāo garrison.
Briefly traveled, there was a dam.
Dug open the solid dam and departed.
Proceeding past the dam, there was the Rúgāo office.
The official in charge, not yet clear of the details.
The boat traveled too slowly.
So stopped the water buffalo.
Reorganized three boats into one group.
Each group divided seven sailors.
Ordered to tow the boats away.
Briefly traveled, people grew tired.
Again, long ropes tied to the buffalo to tow away.
Left and right, plans failed.
Tiredness added to tiredness.
Many people hard to tow.
Tied buffalo, swift journey.
Then people all said.
One buffalo's strength equals a hundred men.
By noon.
On the north bank of the waterway.
Willow trees connected.
At the wèi hour, arrived at the Rúgāo Jiǎn shop, briefly stopped.
North bank of the dug canal.
Shops connected.
The archer Zhàngbù Zhēnmíng and others.
Came from where the ambassador was, saying.
From here, half a lǐ.
At the west end, there is the garrison.
The ambassador, judge, and others reside here.
Not yet gone to the county office.
The ambassador, judge, etc., heard that tribute goods had arrived, so again headed toward the prefecture.
Ordered to prepare the boats.
Also said.
Today, the prefectural envoy came.
Began to supply provisions.
Previously guided the Silla envoys.
And with our country together.
But this year's tribute envoy is called the Silla envoy.
And the reception was neglectful.
Now the ambassador and others.
First came to the garrison.
Already determined that our country and Silla are separate, distant and far apart.
Then the county and prefecture acknowledged and reported it, already completed.
Suddenly hearing this, joyful.
Greatly comforted the weary feelings.
At the shēn hour, the garrison ambassador Liú Miǎn rode a horse.
Came to where the boats were anchored.
Horse groom, followers, about seven or eight people.
Finished inspecting matters and left immediately.
The clerk and others disembarked.
Went to pay respects at the ambassador's place.
Day late, did not travel.
Stayed here overnight.
On the twenty-first day, at the mǎo hour.
The ambassador and below all departed together.
Left and right of the waterway, wealthy homes connected.
Absolutely no obstacles.
Traveled briefly not long.
Homes gradually sparse.
Previously, the garrison had returned to the country.
The ambassador saw us off for about three or four lǐ.
Returned to his own garrison.
From the garrison to the county, two hundred twenty lǐ.
At the sì hour, released the water buffalo.
Each divided into one boat.
Rowed and proceeded.
Absolutely no homes.
At the end of shēn hour, arrived at Yánhǎi Village in Yánhǎi Township.
Stopped to stay.
Mosquitoes and gnats very many.
Hardship boundless.
Set off at midnight.
Salt official boats loaded with salt.
Some three or four boats.
Some four or five boats.
Paired and tied together.
Unbroken for tens of lǐ.
Following along and traveling.
Suddenly seeing, hard to record.
Very marvelous.
On the twenty-second day, at dawn.
All boats tied to water buffalo to pull away.
White geese, white ducks, often many.
There were people's homes connected.
After the sì hour.
Sometimes traveled thirty lǐ.
Only three or four homes.
Presence or absence uncertain.
Entered night, traveled in darkness.
At the zǐ hour, arrived at a village.
Did not know its name.
All boats stayed here overnight.
On the twenty-third day, at the mǎo hour, set off.
The locals reported.
From here to the county, twenty lǐ.
Traveled briefly not long.
Beside the waterway.
There were people raising water birds.
Gathered together in one place.
Not letting them scatter outside.
One place raised over two thousand.
Such kinds.
Exist at river bends.
Bamboo groves exist everywhere.
Bamboo about four zhàng long is considered superior.
Pointed north, flowing forward.
From the first day of boarding the boat.
Mostly pointed west.
Sometimes north.
Sometimes northeast.
Sometimes northwest.
At the chén hour, ahead saw a pagoda.
Immediately asked the locals.
They answered.
This is Xīchí Temple.
Its pagoda is an earthen pagoda.
Has nine stories.
Among the seven official temples, this is one of them.
Proceeded not long.
Arrived at the east end of Hǎilíng County.
The county officials.
One chief official.
One judge.
Military commanders, etc., total seven people.
Not yet clear of their ranks.
Briefly traveled to the river south of the county.
The county magistrate and others came to welcome at the bridge south of Xīchí Temple on the river.
The ambassador, judge, clerk, etc.
Disembarked and went ashore.
Went to the temple to stay overnight.
The county office presented money.
But only invited the visiting study monks.
Still on the boat.
The county people all gathered, competing to see.
The visiting study monk had a stomach ache.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the hour of Chén.
At Xīchí Temple, a lecture on the Awakening of Faith was held.
The Abbot Qiān, along with the former and current Tripiṭaka administrators and others, came aboard the ship.
They inquired after the well-being of the two monks who had come from afar.
Communication was conducted through written brush.
Those monks stayed briefly and then returned.
By the time of Sì hour.
The Ambassador and those below him.
Left the temple and boarded the ship.
Together they set off.
The officials and others from the county.
As they had not shown due diligence in their inquiries.
Dispatched soldiers and others to escort them.
At Shēn hour, they arrived at Yílíng Lodge.
This is a place for lodging officials and guests traveling to and fro.
According to the report, Deputy Envoy Fujiwara no Sadatoshi suddenly fell ill with diarrhea.
All ships stopped and lodged in front of this lodge.
The two monks disembarked to see.
And inquire after the sick.
Immediately upon returning to the ship, they heard that the Deputy Envoy of the fourth ship could not bear even soup or water.
He disembarked and stayed at the house of a local boatman.
The ship carrying the national tribute goods had not yet been unloaded when it completely split apart.
However, both public and private goods suffered no unusual damage.
As there were no welcoming boats, they could not be transported ashore.
On the twenty-fifth day, at Yín hour, they set off.
Everyone was suffering from diarrhea.
The sailing of the ships was not orderly.
Ships that had gone ahead.
Stopped to wait for the later ones.
People from the later ships.
Advanced to the front of the line.
From Hǎilíng County.
It was over fifty lǐ to Yílíng Lodge.
Sixty-five lǐ to the prefecture.
At Sì hour, they arrived at Xiāngōng Abbey.
They proceeded directly without stopping.
At Wèi hour, they stopped east of the Chánzhì Bridge.
North of the bridge was Chánzhì Temple.
During the Enryaku era, the memorial service for the Vice-Envoy's death anniversary.
Was held at this temple.
Three lǐ west from the bridge.
Was Yángzhōu Prefecture.
The Ambassador, to conduct state affairs.
Dispatched the Supervising Official and others to the prefecture, but they were delayed in coming.
At Shēn hour, they set off.
The river was filled with large vessels.
Reed boats.
Small boats, and others.
Too numerous to count.
After Shēn hour, they passed through the eastern water gate of the outer wall.
At Yǒu hour, they stopped at the river north of the city.
The Ambassador and others went ashore to lodge.
They had not yet met with the prefectural authorities.
The Petitioning Monk and the Student Monk, etc.
Had not yet left the ship.
At night, rain fell.
Their hardship was especially severe.
On the twenty-sixth day, at Bū hour.
They disembarked and lodged at an official inn south of the river.
The two monks each occupied separate rooms.
On the twenty-eighth day, after the morning meal, they hired a small boat.
To go toward Língjū Temple.
Halfway there was an obstruction.
They did not enter the temple.
And returned to the official inn.
Not long after.
Monk Quán Cāo and eight other monks from Kāiyuán Temple came.
To inquire after their travel-worn condition.
On the thirtieth day, Monk Zhēn Shùn from Kāiyuán Temple came to inquire.
He wrote with a brush asking the name of the prefectural temple and the Dharma Master's name.
And also presented local products.
On the first day of the eighth month, early morning.
The Ambassador went to the prefectural yamen.
To see Governor Li Xiànggong of Yáng Prefecture.
After the matter was concluded, he returned.
After the morning meal, the Petitioning and Student Monks.
Submitted a petition to the Envoy's yamen.
Requesting to go to Guóqīng Temple in Táizhōu.
And also requesting that sailors Ding Shèng and Komaro be assigned.
To serve as attendants for seeking the Dharma.
In the evening, by order of the Ambassador.
To fulfill vows made at sea.
They went to Kāiyuán Temple.
To look at and decide on a quiet courtyard.
Over thirty senior monks of the Tripiṭaka administration.
All came to inquire after them.
After making a circuit of reverence, they returned to the inn.
On the third day, they requested that the petition for the Petitioning Monk and others to go to Táizhōu.
Be delivered by official dispatch to Yáng Prefecture, which was done.
To have paintings made of the Bodhisattva Myōken.
And the Four Heavenly Kings, painters were sent to the temple.
But due to regulations, foreigners were not permitted to freely enter temple grounds.
The Tripiṭaka administrators, etc.
Did not allow the said images to be painted.
Therefore, an official dispatch was sent to the Xiànggong.
There was no reply yet.
On the fourth day, early morning, there was a reply.
The Ambassador presented local products to Li Xiànggong.
That Xiànggong did not accept them and returned them.
Also, starting today.
The daily provisions for sustenance were not fully provided.
After the morning meal, from Yáng Prefecture.
A follow-up inquiry document was brought.
That document stated.
The Returning Monk Yuánrén.
Novices Wéizhèng and Wéixiǎo.
Sailor Dīng Xióngmǎn, the aforementioned request to go to Guóqīng Temple in Táizhōu to seek a teacher.
Then reside in Táizhōu.
Or, from Táizhōu, to return.
And proceed to the capital.
The Student Monk Yuánzǎi.
Novice Rénhǎo.
Attendant Shǐmǎn.
The aforementioned request to go to Guóqīng Temple in Táizhōu to seek a teacher.
Then reside in Táizhōu.
Or, from Táizhōu, to return.
And proceed to the capital.

In the custom of the Tang country,
whenever a feast is set, besides the food, a separate amount of coin money is reserved.
Just before the feast concludes,
depending on the amount of money,
it is divided equally among the monks according to their number.
However, an additional sum is given
to the person who composed the feast text.
If each monk receives thirty coins,
the composer of the feast text
receives four hundred coins.
This is called "donation money."
It corresponds to what is called almsgiving in our country.
After the feast, everyone rinsed their mouths in the same place
and returned to their quarters.
This is the regular practice in monasteries.
If a donor
intends to provide porridge for the monks the next morning, a notice is circulated in the evening informing them that there will be porridge the next morning.
If someone arranges a feast, no notice is given the evening before,
but on the same day, early in the morning, a notice is circulated
that there is food in the abbot's hall.
If someone comes to the monastery
to request sutra recitation,
they also have someone announce to go to the hall and recite sutras.
In this Yáng Prefecture,
there are over forty monasteries.
When a feast is held at one monastery,
monks from other monasteries are invited in turn to receive the feast and donation.
In this rotating manner,
whenever there is a feast,
the monastery names are recorded,
and monks from other monasteries are invited in order.
This establishes the order of monasteries and the order of monks.
One monastery does it this way,
and the others likewise.
They take turns by monastery order,
and take turns by monk order.
Depending on the abundance or scarcity of feasts, the invitation of monks is not fixed.
If one monastery holds a feast for one day,
it is calculated that monks from the hall monastery and monks in order from this monastery [will attend].
There are also secular-instructing Dharma Masters,
similar to what we call "flying teaching masters" in our country.
They expound the principles of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness in the world,
guiding male and female disciples.
They are called secular-instructing Dharma Masters.
Those who lecture on sutras, treatises, vinaya, commentaries, subcommentaries, etc.,
are called "lecture masters," "venerable masters," or "great virtues."
If they wear patched robes and focus on mind cultivation,
they are called "Chan masters."
They are also called "practitioners."
Those especially proficient in vinaya are called "vinaya great virtues."
Those who lecture on vinaya are called "vinaya lecture masters."
Others are similarly designated.
Since last October,

The Minister ordered seven monasteries

In the custom of the Tang country,
to pray for clear weather, the north end of the road is closed;
to pray for rain, the south end of the road is closed.
It is traditionally said:
When praying for clear weather and closing the north end,
closing the yin allows the yang to flow freely,
which is suitable for clear weather.
When praying for rain and closing the south end,
closing the yang allows the yin to flow freely,
which is suitable for rainfall.

The monastic administrator

In general, in this Táng country,

a south wind blew somewhat strongly.

In the afternoon, a strong south wind blew.
On the twenty-second, there was rain.
In the shēn hour,

On the twenty-third,
there were clouds and a south wind.
On the twenty-fourth, there was misty rain.

The cables broke.

This ship often had hidden reefs.

Finally,

Like walls surrounding.

To the east and north.

All day the northeast wind blew.

Overcast, rain, north wind.

At sunset.
On the ship.

One sailor.

The third day.
The wind direction did not change.
From the southwestern harbor of Rǔshān.
We hoisted the sails and set off.

At noon, the wind stopped.

Starting from tomorrow.

The sixth day.

The Silla interpreter Dàoxuán.
Went to the yāyá's residence.
After the meal.

The Vinaya Master Jièmíng.

On the seventh day, it rained.

From this day until the thirteenth.

Encountered headwinds.

Since arriving at this anchorage.
At night, there was thunder and heavy rain.

The aforementioned people.

On the seventeenth and eighteenth days.

The shrine at the ship's bow.
The planks of its roof covering.

Their whereabouts unknown.

Unable to control themselves.
The twentieth day.
A west wind blew.

Arranging the sails.

Not long after.

About six inches wide.
Over three zhàng long.

Also, offering silks to be presented upon reaching our country.
We would specially erect a shrine.

If we made a replacement.

So we could advance early.

A wind arose from the northwest.
Slightly moving the ship.

Shifting and unsettled.
From before until today.

The first day of the sixth month.
The sky was slightly clear.

Not losing.

Sometimes blowing, sometimes not.

Three or four times already.

From Shàocūnpǔ.

All the people on the ship.

On the fifth day, at dawn.

Unable to cross the sea,

On the sixth day, a fierce wind blew sharply.

On the seventh day,

We raised the sails and proceeded.

The fierce wind was intense.
This Chìshān is entirely of high, elegant rocky cliffs.
It is located in Chìshān Village, Qīngníng Township, Wéndēng County.

To the south, west, and north,

Not ceasing for a moment.

Repaired the small boats.

On the fifteenth day,

Northwest wind blew.

Yíng Mountain,

Heard from an old elder,

The three monks, for the purpose of going to Tiāntāi,

Remained at Chìshān Monastery.

South far, north near.

Recorded according to the oral account of the Silla monk, Hēshàng Shènglín.

The lecture ceremony at Chìshān Monastery
At the hour of Chén,
the lecture bell was struck.
It was struck to alert the assembly.
After the bell,
after a long while,
the great assembly entered the hall.
Once the assembly was settled, the bell was struck, and the lecturer entered the hall.
Ascending the high seat,
the great assembly in unison
chanted the Buddha’s name.
The melody entirely followed Sillan style,
unlike Táng pronunciation.
After the lecturer ascended the seat,
the chanting of the Buddha’s name ceased.
Then, a junior monk performed a chant,
entirely in Táng style,
reciting lines such as “How in this sutra,” etc., one verse.
Up to “May the Buddha reveal the subtle and secret phrases,”
the great assembly in unison chanted, “Incense of precepts, incense of meditation, incense of liberation,” etc.
After the chant and hymn,
the lecturer announced
the sutra’s title.
Then he began the topic,
dividing it into three sections.
After explaining the title,
the precentor came forward,
before the high seat,
announced the reason for the gathering and the names of the donors,
and listed the donated items.
Then, he presented the list
to the lecturer.
The lecturer, holding the yak-tail whisk,
announced each donor’s name one by one.
He then made a personal vow.
After the vow,
the discussants raised questions on the topics.
During the questioning,
the lecturer raised the whisk.
Hearing the questioner’s words,
after the question was raised,
he lowered the whisk.
Then raised it again.
After thanking for the question, he answered.
Questions and answers were exchanged in writing,
similar to in our country.
However, the difficulty
lay in the slightly different ceremony.
After slapping the side of the hand three times,
they explained before the assembly.
Suddenly pointing and raising objections,
their voices were like those of greatly angry people, shouting and disputing.
The lecturer’s family’s objections
were only answered, not countered.
After the discussion,
they entered the text to expound the sutra.
After the lecture,
the great assembly in unison chanted long praises.
Within the praises,
there were dedication verses.
The lecturer descended from the seat.
One monk chanted the verse “The world is like space,”
the melody somewhat resembling that of our country.
The lecturer ascended the ritual platform.
One monk chanted the threefold homage, after which
the lecturer and the great assembly in unison
left the hall and returned to their rooms.
There was also a review lecturer,
south of the high seat.
The junior lecturer then discussed the text lectured by the lecturer the previous day.
As for the meaning of the assembly,
after the lecturer read the text and explained its meaning,
the review lecturer also read.
After reading all the text lectured the previous day,
the lecturer then read the next section.
Every day was like this.
Silla's Daily Lecture Ceremony: At the hour of chén, the bell is struck.
After a long strike,
the lecturer and the assistant lecturer, two persons, enter the hall.
The assembly enters first and sits in rows.
The lecturer recites the verse for the master's entrance into the hall.
The assembly chants in unison.
They praise the Buddha's name with a long, drawn-out tone.
The lecturer ascends the northern seat.
The assistant lecturer ascends the southern seat.
The praise of the Buddha then ceases.
At that time, a monk of lower rank performs a chant.
It is a verse line such as "How in this sutra," etc.
After the chant is performed,
the southern seat intones the title of the sutra.
This is called intoning the sutra with a long, drawn-out tone.
The melody often has many twists and turns during the intonation of the sutra.
The assembly scatters flowers three times.
Each time flowers are scattered,
there are respective verses recited.
After the sutra is intoned,
the title is intoned again in a shorter melody.
The lecturer opens the sutra's contents.
He divides it into three gates.
He expounds the general meaning of the sutra.
After explaining the sutra's title,
there is the monastic overseer.
He reads aloud the document stating the matter and its origin.
In that document,
the principle of impermanence is fully recorded.
The merits of the deceased.
The number of days since the passing.

Míng Qǐ Jǐ.

Silla's Sutra Recitation Ceremony.
In the Great Táng, it is called "niànjīng" (chanting sutras).
After striking the bell to settle the assembly,
a monk of lower rank
rises, strikes the wooden block, and intones: "All be reverent, respectfully pay homage to the eternal Three Jewels."
Next, a monk performs a chant.
It is a two-line verse such as "The Tathāgata's wonderful colored body," etc.
The melody and rhythm are the same as in Táng.
During the performance of the chant,
one person holds the incense cup.
He passes in front of the seats of the assembly.
He walks quickly and then stops.
The assembly chants in unison,
reciting the title "Mahāprajñāpāramitā" several tens of times.
There is one master
who states the reason for the sutra recitation.
The assembly chants the sutra in unison.
Sometimes they follow the sutra text,
sometimes they do not follow the sutra text.
After chanting the sutra,
the guiding master alone intones: "I take refuge in the Buddha,
I take refuge in the Dharma,
I take refuge in the Sangha."
Next, he invokes the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The guiding master intones:
"Námó (Homage to) the Twelve Great Vows."
The assembly says:
"Yàoshī Liúlíguāng Fó (Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha)."
The guiding master says: "Námó Yàoshī."
The assembly chants in unison:
"Liúlíguāng Fó."
The guiding master says: "Námó the Great Compassionate."
The assembly chants in unison:
"Guānshìyīn Púsà (Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva)."
The rest are all like this.
After paying homage to the Buddha,
the guiding master alone makes the dedicatory prayer and transfers of merit.
The transfer of merit is somewhat lengthy.
After the transfer of merit,
the guiding master says:
"Develop the mind (of enlightenment)."
The assembly in unison also says:
"Develop the mind."
Next, the guiding master intones: "The making of vows is now completed.
We bow our heads in reverence to the Three Jewels."
Next, the donor sits holding the offering items.
The guiding master gives the blessing and then they disperse.

Requesting to be granted an official permit to proceed to Wǔtái and other famous mountains, and to various places to visit sacred traces, seek teachers, and study the Dharma: Monk Ennin, disciples Wéizhèng, Wéixiǎo, attendant Dīng Xióngmǎn, along with personal robes, alms bowl, etc.

The above: We, Ennin and others, with great resolve, admire the Buddhist teachings and practice the Buddha Way. From afar, we heard that in China, Wǔtái and other places are the source of Buddhism and the transforming grounds of great sages. Eminent monks from the Western Heavens cross dangers from afar to reach the land of Hàn; famous worthies travel here and attain the Way. We, Ennin and others, cannot restrain our admiration and longing, crossing the seas to visit and seek. We have not yet fulfilled our long-held wish. In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Kāichéng era, we arrived at Chìshān, Xīnluó Monastery in Qīngníng Township, Wéndēng County. Separated from our living connections by the vast ocean, we forget our native soil on the seashore. Fortunately, we are allowed freedom to travel east and west, arriving in your benevolent realm. Now wishing to go to various places to pay respects and visit sacred traces, seek teachers and study the Dharma, we fear that the prefectures, counties, garrison towns, city gates, streets, passes, ferries, postal stations, village temples, lodgings, etc., along the way will not be familiar with our purpose. We humbly hope to be granted an official permit to serve as proof. Respectfully detailed as above. Humbly request your disposition. The memorial is as stated before. Respectfully submitted.

Has a devout heart.
Loves discussing principles, and seeing monks from afar, attentively inquired and comforted.
At mealtime, the Deputy Military Commissioner.
Sent an official to summon [us] into the prefecture to the reporting office for the meal.
Six or seven officials.
Food and drink were proper.
On the twenty-fourth day, the Spring Festival, the day of the "Music of Breaking the Formation."
A banquet was set up in the prefectural polo field.
At dawn.
The annual director and kitchen steward.
Led [us] to be accommodated at the New Silla Courtyard.
On the twenty-fifth day, to request the official permit.
Again drafted a petition to present to the Minister.
Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
I, Yuánrén, and others,
with hearts yearning for the sacred sites,
crossed the sea to seek them out.
We wished to go to Táishān,
to practice the Way there through the summer, and later travel to various places,
seeking teachers and requesting the Dharma.
Fearing the road was long and the season hot,
we might not fulfill our original wish.
Previously, we had a prefectural document,
fully stating the reasons. We humbly hope the Minister, in his benevolence,
will specially grant an official travel permit,
so that our sincere wish may be fulfilled,
and we may soon proceed on our forward journey.
We humbly request your decision.
The 25th day of the third month of the fifth year of the Kāichéng era. Submitted by the Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
From Dēng Prefecture, Wéndēng County,
to this place, Qīng Prefecture.
For three or four years now,
locust disasters have arisen.
They have consumed the five grains; officials and commoners alike suffer hunger and poverty.
In the Dēng Prefecture area,
they specifically eat acorns as food.
Traveling monks and others
passing through this difficult place find food hard to obtain.
Millet is eighty wen per dou,
non-glutinous rice is one hundred wen per dou.
With no food to eat,
I then prepared a petition
to present to Vice Military Commissioner Attendant Gentleman Zhāng,
begging for food provisions.
The Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén,
requests the alms of food provisions.
I, Yuánrén, and others,
having traveled far from our native country,
seeking out the Buddhist teaching,
in order to request an official travel permit,
have no fixed direction,
making home wherever we are. Hunger is hard to bear.
Because our speech sounds are different,
we cannot specifically beg. We humbly hope,
in your benevolent grace, to bestow the surplus from the fragrant storehouse,
granting it to a poor monk from a foreign land.
Previously, we received one portion;
now we trouble you again,
deeply feeling shame and remorse.
Respectfully sending my disciple Wéizhèng with this petition.
Respectfully submitted.
The 25th day of the third month of the fifth year of the Kāichéng era. Submitted by the Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
Attendant Gentleman,
Attendant Gentleman,
bestowed and gave three dou of non-glutinous rice, three dou of flour, and three dou of millet.
I then prepared a petition of thanks.
The Japanese monk Yuánrén respectfully thanks
the Attendant Gentleman for his benevolent provision of rice and flour.
I cannot fully express my gratitude and reverence.
It is difficult to adequately convey my thanks.
My humble feelings
cannot bear the sincerity of gratitude and shame. Respectfully I present this petition to express my thanks.
Not elaborating further, respectfully submitted.
The 25th day of the third month of the fifth year of the Kāichéng era. Submitted by the Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
Attendant Gentleman.
On the 27th,
I sent Wéizhèng to the main administrative office
to inquire about the official travel permit matter.
The official in charge of the case reported, saying:
"A decision has already been made.
To grant the official travel permit.
On one hand, issue the official permit;
on the other hand, report it to the throne.
Wait until the day after tomorrow,
during the morning session at the yamen, the Minister will sign and affix his seal,
then have it delivered."
The 28th, the beginning of summer.
The weather was overcast.
Wáng Lǐwǔ, the deputy official of Dēng Prefecture, came to the monastery to visit.
Then I heard:
"The Prince of Bóhǎi
arrived the other day,
intending to return to his homeland.
He awaits the imperial envoy to arrive before departing.
He is staying at this monastery for the summer provisions."
The monastery had a general invitation for the meal offering.
We went there for the midday meal.
There were about fifty monks.
On the 29th, I prepared a petition to present to the Minister, begging for alms food.
The Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén,
requests the alms of food provisions.
I, Yuánrén, and others,
having traveled far across the vast waves,
to seek out the Buddhist teaching,
my humble self is most fortunate
to have traveled to the honorable territory of the Minister.
Because we are pressed by travel,
alms food is scarce and we suffer hunger.
Our speech sounds are different,
and there is nowhere to beg.
We humbly hope
the Minister, in his benevolence,
will bestow and give food provisions,
nurturing and supporting this poor monk.
Truly, the merit of your charitable giving
compares to that of Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya,
and the virtue of your vast aid vies with that of Bākula. I cannot bear the sincerity of my reverence and earnestness.
Respectfully I present this petition to make my request.
Humbly, my fear and trepidation increase. Not elaborating further, respectfully submitted.
The 29th day of the third month of the fifth year of the Kāichéng era. Submitted by the Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
Minister.
I sent my disciple Wéizhèng
to have him present the petition.
Immediately, I received a reply, saying:
"Tomorrow there will be a decision."
On the 30th,
I went to the invitation of the Recluse Xiāo,
to his residence for the midday meal.
Then I heard that the Military Commissioner had recorded the reasons for the arrival of the Dharma-seeking monks and reported it to the Son of Heaven, which was completed.
On the first day of the fourth month,
during the morning session at the yamen, I received the official travel permit.
The Minister bestowed and gave three bolts of cloth and six catties of tea.
At the mealtime, this monastery had a meal offering.
Today is the birthday of the Minister's son,
so they set up a long-life meal offering.
On the second day, early morning, at Administrative Assistant Xiāo's residence, we ate congee.
Then I entered the prefecture to present a petition thanking the Minister for the bestowed items,
and also to take leave of the Minister.
The Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén,
humbly received the Minister's benevolent provision,
bestowing and giving three bolts of cloth and six catties of tea.
My humble feelings cannot fully express my gratitude and reverence.
Respectfully I present this petition to express my thanks.
Not elaborating further, respectfully submitted.
The second day of the fourth month of the fifth year of the Kāichéng era. Submitted by the Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén.
The Minister summoned me to the front of the yamen and conveyed a message:
"What was bestowed is meager and little,
not worth mentioning.
Thank you for your trouble. Reverend, go well."
Next, I entered the courtyard of Vice Military Commissioner Attendant Gentleman Zhāng to bid farewell.
The Attendant Gentleman summoned me into the yamen,
served tea, cakes, and food.
We drank tea and bid farewell.
The Attendant Gentleman came to the monastery,
to attend Zhào Déjì's invitation for a meal offering.
Towards evening,
a staff officer of the military headquarters bestowed and gave two dou of grain and rice,
and two dou of small beans for donkey fodder.
At dusk,
I entered the residence of the staff officer of the military headquarters,
to thank him for bestowing travel provisions and to bid the staff officer farewell.
On the third day, at daybreak, we departed.
The staff officer of the military headquarters assigned one traveling official
to see us past the city gate.
The military headquarters, from the time of our first meeting,
was extremely cordial and attentive.
While at the monastery,
every day there were gracious bestowals,
and inquiries and concern never ceased.
At the time of our departure,
they assigned someone to see us off on our journey,
and also showed us the way.
Today, the Minister and the Army Supervisor
went to various temples to pray for rain.
From the monastery,
we passed northwest of the prefectural city.
Ten li from the city is Yáo Mountain.
On the mountain is the Temple of King Yáo.
In the past, King Yáo traveled through this region; where he passed,
they subsequently built this temple.
It is traditionally said:
Whenever they pray for rain,
they invariably receive rainfall.
Exiting the city, we headed north for twenty li,
arriving at Shíyáng Village in Yìdū County, at the Chén family's for a meal.
The host was fair-minded.
After the midday meal, we traveled northwest for fifteen li,
arriving at Zīshuǐ Post Station in Línzī County.
Traveling west for twenty-five li,
we arrived at the Wáng family east of Jīnlǐng Post Station to lodge.
The host was honest and good-natured by disposition,
and treated guests with cordiality.
Looking west, we saw Chángbái Mountain in the distance.
On the fourth day, at daybreak, we departed.
Traveling west for sixteen li,
we entered a small path looking towards Chángbái Mountain.
Heading west for five li,
we arrived at Zhāngzhào Village in Zīchuān County, Zī Prefecture.
We entered the Zhào family for a meal.
The host was extremely poor,
with no rice to eat.
His heart held no malice.
After the midday meal, we traveled northwest for thirty li,
arriving at Gǔxiàn Village in Chángshān County to lodge at the Lǚ family's.
The host was a blacksmith.
He was originally from Pèi Prefecture.
Fair-minded and possessing a mind for the Way.
On the fifth day, we set off early in the morning.
Traveling ten li northwest,
we arrived at Chángshān County.
From the west of the county, we traveled ten li,
reaching Zhāng Lǐ's relay station.
The host was very attentive.
After the morning meal, we traveled fifteen li westward,
arriving at the eastern side of Chángbái Mountain.
It was around the hour of the Monkey (3–5 p.m.).
At the front of Xiānréntái, in the village of Shǐ's family in Bùcūn, we drank tea.
We inquired about Lǐquán Temple.
The host replied,
"From Bùcūn, head directly west for fifteen li,
and you will reach Lǐquán Temple."
We then proceeded directly west into the mountains.
We took a wrong path and traveled over ten li.
There were many branching paths.
We did not know which direction to go.
As it was getting dark, we returned to the Shǐ family in Bùcūn to stay for the night.
Dogs barked all night long.
We were frightened and could not sleep.
On the morning of the sixth day,
the host offered us porridge.
He also assigned a person to accompany us,
showing us the way.
We headed directly west,
entered a valley, crossed over a high ridge,
and descended a slope westward before finally reaching Lǐquán Temple.
We drank tea in the orchard.
Traveling two li further south,
we arrived at Lǐquán Temple's relay station for the midday meal.
After the meal, we toured the temple grounds.
We paid respects to the portrait of Master Zhìgōng.
It was enshrined in the Liúlí Hall.
The door pillars, rafters, and steps
were all constructed from green stone.
Precious banners of wondrous colors,
the rarest treasures of the world,
were displayed throughout the hall.
Master Zhìgōng
was an incarnation of the Eleven-Faced Bodhisattva.
The story of his origins is inscribed on a stele.
The Master
was a native of Jīnchéng during the Sòng Dynasty.
He manifested his spiritual presence here on Chángbái Mountain.
After his nirvana,
his physical body disappeared, its whereabouts unknown.
Only an image was made.
The entire nation reveres him.
West of the hall, by the edge of the valley,
there is the Lǐquán Well.
In former times, a spring gushed forth here,
with a fragrant aroma and sweet taste.
Those who drank it
were cured of illness and had their lifespan increased.
Since then, it has been named Lǐquán Temple (Sweet Spring Temple).
After the Master's nirvana,
the spring water dried up completely,
leaving only an empty well.
Now, above the well,
a small hall has been built,
and another image of the Master has been made.
In front of the image, inside the hall,
there is a stone well,
over five feet deep.
Now it is seen to have no water.
South of the temple is a peak
named Lóngtái (Dragon Terrace).
It rises alone above the multitude of peaks.
According to maps and records,
a dragon was once seen dancing on its summit, and this was reported to the emperor.
By imperial decree,
it was renamed Lóngtái Temple.
Later, because of the spring's emergence,
it was renamed Lǐquán Temple.
To the east, south, and west,
lofty peaks form a continuous barrier.
To the north, it is open and expansive,
with no hills or mounds.
The temple buildings are dilapidated,
and there is not much pure food.
The sacred sites are in decline,
with no one to repair or maintain them.
The temple has fifteen estates,
which are still numerous today.
Originally, there were about a hundred monks on the monastic path here.
Now, they have dispersed according to their circumstances.
Those currently residing at the temple
number over thirty.
The monk in charge of provisions
led us to the Xīnluó Courtyard for lodging.
On the morning of the seventh day,
after eating porridge in the main hall, we set off.
The provisioner and the other monks urged us to stay,
saying, "Tomorrow the temple will hold a grand feast.
Why leave so early?"
We replied that we wished to reach Táishān early and could not delay.
We exited the temple gate
and traveled fifteen li north,
arriving at Lǐquán Temple's estate for the midday meal.
We then traveled twenty li directly west,
arriving at Zhāngqiū County.
From the west of the county, we traveled fifteen li,
crossing the Jì River ferry crossing.
People of the time call it Jìkǒu.
From the crossing, we traveled half a li northwest,
and stayed at the Wáng family's home.
The host was fair-minded.
On the eighth day, we set off early.
Traveling twenty-five li directly west,
we arrived at Línjì County and entered the Yǐn family's home for the midday meal.
We then set off again.
A merchant gave us five *shēng* of rice.
Passing through the market, we traveled thirty li directly west.
At the hour of the Monkey (3–5 p.m.),
we arrived at Zhīlóng Village in Línyì County and stayed at the Zhāng family's home.
In the evening, rain began to fall.
The host was fair-minded.
On the morning of the ninth day, rain continued to fall,
so we could not set off.
After the morning meal, the rain cleared and we set off.
Traveling fifteen li directly west,
we arrived at Gǔ County.
This was the former Línyì County.
The city walls
were in ruins, with not a single government building remaining.
Temples from earlier generations were destroyed.
Buddha images sat exposed.
The land had been turned back into farmland.
It was truly lamentable.
We traveled fifteen li directly west,
arriving at the Yuán River ferry crossing.
Crossing the river and traveling ten li,
we arrived at Luántáng Village in Yǔchéng County and stayed at the Lǐfǔ family's home.
The host had a devout mind.
On the tenth day, we set off at dawn.
Traveling forty li directly west,
at the hour of the Goat (1–3 p.m.),
we arrived at Yǔchéng County.
In the county market, millet was 45 *wen* per *dǒu*,
non-glutinous rice was 100 *wen* per *dǒu*,
small beans were 15 *wen* per *dǒu*,
and flour was 70–80 *wen*.
Passing west of the city, we traveled ten li,
arriving at Xiāngōng Village and staying at the Zhào family's home.
All night there was thunder, lightning, hail, and rain.
By dawn, the thunder and rain had stopped.
The host did not have a devout mind.
On the eleventh day, we set off at the hour of the Rabbit (5–7 a.m.).
Traveling thirty li directly west,
at noon,
we arrived at the Huáng Hé (Yellow River) ferry crossing.
People of the time call it Yàojiākǒu.
The water was turbid yellow, flowing swiftly like an arrow.
The river was about one *chō* and five *dan* wide.
It flows eastward.
The source of the Yellow River is in the Kūnlún Mountains.
It has nine bends.
Six bends are in the Tǔfān Kingdom,
and three bends are in the Great Táng Kingdom.
At the ferry crossing, on the northern and southern banks,
there are ferry crossings on each side.
The city walls extend over four *chō* north and south,
and about one *chō* east and west.
At this Yàojiākǒu,
there are many boats eager to ferry people back and forth.
Each person pays five *wen*.
A donkey costs fifteen *qián*.
The southern bank belongs to Yǔchéng County in Qí Prefecture.
The northern bank belongs to the southern border of Dé Prefecture.
Crossing to the northern bank, we had our midday meal.
The four of us each ate four bowls of flour porridge.
The host was astonished,
saying, "Eating so much cold food,
I fear it will not be digested."
We traveled thirty-five li directly west.
At the hour of the Monkey (3–5 p.m.),
we arrived at Zhàoguǎn Village in Píngyuán County, Dé Prefecture, and stayed at the Zhào family's home.
The host did not have a devout mind.
On the twelfth day, we set off early.
Traveling forty li directly west,
we arrived at Xíngkāi Village in Xiàjīn County, Pèi Prefecture, and had our midday meal at the Zhào family's home.
The host had a devout mind.
He offered a vegetarian meal,
with ample vegetables, and we were fully satisfied.
After the meal, we set off.
Traveling thirty li westward,
we arrived at the border of Xiàjīn County.
We stayed at the Sūn family's home in Mèngjiāzhuāng.
The host had a devout mind.
On the thirteenth day, we departed.
Traveling thirty-five li westward,
we arrived at Wángyān Village, at the Wang family's home, to break our fast.
The host, Zúdào, with a devout heart, offered a vegetarian meal.
After the meal, we traveled thirty-five li westward.
At the hour of Shēn, we reached Tángzhōu City and lodged at Kāiyuán Temple.
It was said
that the Vice Censor-in-Chief, Shēn, the Military Commissioner,
had newly opened an ordination platform at Kāiyuán Temple.
Notices were posted throughout the streets and alleys,
to inform the people.
More than four hundred monks had come from various prefectures to receive the precepts.
Yesterday, the ordination platform concluded,
and the newly ordained monks had all dispersed.
Those seen not yet departed
numbered only over thirty.
The temple administrators
recorded in detail the circumstances of the Japanese monks' arrival
and reported it to the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
On the fourteenth day,
during the morning session, we entered the prefecture to pay respects to the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
At the Vice Censor-in-Chief's residence,
a vegetarian meal for ten monks was arranged.
We then attended the Vice Censor-in-Chief's invitation
and dined at the Commissioner's residence.
After the meal, we returned to stay at the temple.
In the evening,
we entered the ordination platform courtyard
and saw the newly established ordination platform.
It was built with bricks in two tiers.
The lower tier was twenty-five chi square on each side,
the upper tier fifteen chi square on each side.
The height difference between the tiers was two chi and five cun.
The upper tier was two chi and five cun high, and the platform's color was bluish-green.
People at the time said
it was meant to resemble lapis lazuli.
On the fifteenth day,
we broke our fast at the Liú family's home within the city.
The meal was proper.
After the meal, we entered Shànguāng Temple to see the nuns' ordination platform.
Inside the hall, banners were hung and mats spread.
The ground was demarcated with ropes, without constructing a platform.
It was simply laid out on level ground.
It was said that starting tomorrow,
the ordination ceremonies could proceed.
During the evening session, we entered the prefecture to bid farewell to the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
On the sixteenth day, at dawn, we departed.
Traveling twenty li westward,
we reached Hézhāngliú Village in Qīnghé County and broke our fast at the Liú family's home.
We ate elm leaf soup.
Although the host did not understand Buddhism,
he personally offered a vegetarian meal to the monks for breaking our fast.
After the meal, we departed.
Traveling forty li northwest,
we arrived at Zhàogù Village in Nángōng County, Jìzhōu, and stayed at the Zhào family's home.
The host was honest.
On the seventeenth day, early in the morning,
the host offered congee and rice.
Traveling fifteen li due north,
then fifteen li northwest,
we reached Nángōng County, entered the city, and broke our fast at the Zhāng family's home.
Exiting the city, we traveled fifty li northwest.
Settlements were sparse.
We reached Tángyáng County
and entered the city to lodge at Juéguàn Temple.
The temple buildings were dilapidated,
with no resident monks.
There was only one monk in charge of the temple.
He was not attentive to guests.
The rooms and beds
were not properly arranged at all.
On the eighteenth day, at dawn, we departed.
Traveling thirty li due west,
we reached Xīnhékǒu.
Entering the city, we broke our fast at the Nán family's home.
Exiting through the west gate,
we crossed the Xīnhé Bridge and traveled thirty li due west.
The plains stretched far and wide,
with settlements extremely sparse.
We reached Níngjìn County in Zhàozhōu and lodged at Dōngtángchéng Temple.
The temple was extremely poor and desolate; the monks' minds were vulgar and lowly.
On the nineteenth day, at the hour of Chén,
we departed, passing through the city and traveling fifteen li northwest,
to Qínqiū Village, breaking our fast at the Liú family's home.
Although the host was poor,
he offered a vegetarian meal.
At noon, we departed.
Traveling twenty-five li northwest,
the heat was like steam.
We reached Zhàozhōu and lodged at Nán Kāiyuán Temple.
The buildings were dilapidated,
but the Buddha images were dignified.
The resident monks were mean-spirited
and wary of visiting monks.
On the twentieth day, at dawn, we ate congee.
Traveling forty li northwest,
we reached Luánchéng County, Zhènzhōu, and broke our fast at the Sūn family's home outside the city.
Traveling thirty li northwest,
we reached Zuòhù Post Station in Dàkuò County, Zhènzhōu, and stayed at the Dīng family's home.
The host had a thieving heart, scheming against people.
On the twenty-first day, we departed early.
Traveling thirty li due north,
we reached the Military Commissioner's headquarters of Zhènzhōu.
Entering the city, we went to Jīnshā Chán Cloister in the southwest.
No meal was offered for breaking our fast.
There were two monks
who were angry and arrogant toward guests.
They refused us several times,
but we forced our way into the cloister to prepare a meal.
When the host returned,
he,
personally made noodles for the visiting monks.
After the meal, we traveled twenty li due north,
to Shǐzhuāng and stayed at the Yáng family's home.
This estate belonged to the former Military Commissioner of Zhènzhōu,
the Grand Marshal Wáng.
The Grand Marshal's tomb shrine is located within.
Family members of the current Military Commissioner are present guarding the tomb.
There is a military officer surnamed Liú
managing the tomb shrine, which is exquisite.
One li to the south,
a stele hall was built,
surrounded by high walls,
not allowing entry.
Since the Grand Marshal's passing,
three generations have passed.
The host had a devout heart
and was attentive to guests.
On the twenty-second day, early in the morning,
the host offered congee.
Traveling twenty li due north,
we reached Nánjiē Village and broke our fast at the Liú family's home.
The host had long been devout,
always setting out vegetarian meals
to供养 monks,
without limiting the number.
Shortly after entering the house,
he served a meal.
The women of the house came out several times to comfort the guests.
After the meal, we drank tea.
Traveling twenty-five li due north,
we reached Xíngtáng County in Zhènzhōu.
Entering the city, we lodged at Xī Chán Cloister.
There were over twenty Chán monks,
their minds extremely agitated and chaotic.
On the twenty-third day, early in the morning, we ate congee.
Traveling twenty-five li northwest,
we reached Huángshān Bāhuì Temple to break our fast.
We ate coarse rice.
People at the time called it the "Upper Room."
The Common Cloister always had congee and rice.
Regardless of whether monks or laypeople gathered,
they could stay overnight.
If there was food, it was given;
if there was no food, it was not given.
It did not hinder monks or laypeople from coming to stay.
Hence it was called the Common Cloister.
In the cloister, there were two monks:
one open-hearted,
one depressed.
There was a yellow-haired dog
that barked and bit at laypeople,
undeterred by being beaten with a stick.
When it saw monks,
whether resident or guest,
it wagged its tail and was gentle and tame.
After the meal, heading northwest,
we entered the mountains, traveling through valleys.
People at the time called it
Guóxìn Mountain.
Traveling twenty li from the Upper Room,
we reached Liúshǐ Common Cloister to stay.
There we met Monk Yìshēn from Jīngé Temple on Wǔtái Mountain, returning to the mountain after seeking oil in Shēnzhōu.
Fifty donkeys
carried sesame oil away.
We also saw Monk Jùjiān and three others from Guóqīng Temple on Tiāntāi Mountain,
heading to Wǔtái, who informed us:
"At Guóqīng Temple on Tiāntāi Mountain,
there is one Japanese monk,
one disciple novice,
and one attendant.
They are currently residing there."
On the twenty-fourth day, the sky was overcast.
We departed, traveling through valleys
twenty-five li northwest.
We encountered a shepherd driving about five hundred sheep.
Crossing a ridge,
we reached Liǎnglǐng Common Cloister.
The cloister head was absent,
so we prepared our own food.
The cloister had long had no congee or rice
due to recent years of insect disasters,
and now there was no grain.
After the meal, we traveled through valleys,
thirty li northwest,
to Guǒyuàn Common Cloister to stay.
Thunder rumbled, and rain fell.
On the 25th, it rained.
Pǔtōng Monastery.
In the deep mountains, there is no congee or rice.
We ate a few beans as a meal.
From Zhàozhōu onward until this place,
for three or four years, there have been locust disasters.
The five grains have not ripened.
Food is hard to come by.
After the midday meal, the rain stopped, and we searched for the valley heading west.
We traveled thirty lǐ.
Arrived at Xiè Pǔtōng Monastery.
We made a pilgrimage to Wǔtái Shān.
Those who came to make offerings—monks, nuns, and laywomen—
numbered over a hundred people in total.
We stayed overnight together at the monastery.
On the 26th, the sky cleared.
After eating congee,
we headed west through the mountain valley for twenty lǐ.
Arrived at Jìngshuǐ Pǔtōng Monastery and had a meal.
The monastery was impoverished.
The mountain wind gradually turned cool.
Green pines stretched across the ridges.
We crossed two ridges.
Traveling west for thirty lǐ, we arrived at Tángchéng Pǔtōng Monastery.
Passing west of the monastery,
the ridges were high and the valleys deep.
Emerald peaks spewed clouds.
Streams poured down green currents.
From Tángchéng, we traveled west for fifteen lǐ.
At the shēn hour (3–5 p.m.),
we arrived at Lóngquán Pǔtōng Monastery to stay overnight.
Behind the hill, in the Dragon Hall,
a spring gushed forth, clear and cold.
The monastery was near this spring,
so it was called Lóngquán Pǔtōng Monastery.
The monastery had rice and congee.
On the 27th, we set out.

He was seventy years old,

People said
that despite his advanced age, his complexion was robust,
