We opened the hall and reverently paid homage to the great statue of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Its countenance was majestic,
incomparably dignified and solemn.
The statue riding a lion
filled the five-bay hall.
The lion's vital spirit,
its bones vividly rendered,
gave it a sense of movement as if about to step forward.
Its mouth seemed moist with breath.
Gazing at it for a long time,
it truly appeared to be in motion.
An elder monk said:
"When this Bodhisattva was first being made,
each time it was completed, it would crack.
Six times it was crafted,
and six times it cracked and collapsed.
The master craftsman, distressed, said:
'With this singular talent of mine,
known throughout the land,
all acknowledge its unique excellence.
In my lifetime of crafting Buddha images,
I have never seen one crack or damage.
Now, in making this image,
I have observed fasting and purity of heart,
exerting the utmost of my skill and artistry,
hoping to make it an object of veneration for all under heaven,
specifically as a focus for arousing the bodhi-mind.
Now, having crafted it six times,
and six times it has shattered,
it must indeed be that it does not accord with the Great Sage's mind.
If this is truly so,
I humbly pray
that the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva
personally manifest His true form for me,
that I may behold His golden countenance,
and then model and craft accordingly.'
No sooner had he made this vow
than, opening his eyes, he saw
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva riding a golden lion,
appearing before him.
After a long while, riding a five-colored cloud,
He soared into the sky and flew away.
The craftsman, having seen the true form,
was filled with joy and wept with emotion.
Only then did he realize his previous attempts were incorrect.
He then altered the original design,
its proportions and size,
and the likeness of the countenance,
adopting the appearance he had witnessed.
On the seventh attempt, he crafted this image,
and it no longer cracked or damaged.
Every task became easy,
and all that was needed was fulfilled.
After the man completed this image
and installed it in this hall,
tears flowed from the statue's eyes, glistening,
and it said:
'Most wondrous!
What I have never seen before,
now I have seen.
May I, life after life, epoch after epoch, always be a disciple of Mañjuśrī.'
Having spoken, his life ended.
Afterwards,
this image frequently emitted light and repeatedly manifested spiritual auspices.
Whenever there was an auspicious sign,
it was fully recorded and reported to the throne.
An imperial decree bestowed a kāṣāya robe,
which is now seen draped upon the Bodhisattva's form
—this is one of them.
Therefore, each year, imperial envoys deliver a hundred kāṣāya robes,
conferring them upon the mountain monks.
Each year, imperial envoys, under separate decree, deliver incense and flowers,
precious canopies,
pearl banners and canopies,
jade pendants,
precious pearls,
seven-treasure crowns,
gold-inlaid incense burners,
large and small bright mirrors,
flowered carpets,
fine white cotton cloth,
rare artificial flowers and fruits, and so forth.
Gradually, these have accumulated greatly.
They are displayed within the hall,
but cannot all be accommodated.
The remainder are all stored in the treasury,
where they are kept in reserve.
Furthermore, from various circuits, prefectures, government offices, official and private donors,
the offerings sent each year are beyond count.
Now, in all the temples of Wǔtái,
the images of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva that are made
all follow the model of this sacred image.
Yet, they achieve only one part in a hundred of its excellence.
Inside and outside the hall,
seven-treasure parasols
hang above the Bodhisattva's head.
Preciously colored flower banners,
extraordinary pearl garlands, and the like
fill the hall, displayed throughout.
Mirrors adorned with treasures,
large and small, are too numerous to count.
Exiting to the north of the hall,
I beheld the Northern Terrace and Eastern Terrace.
Their rounded summits rose high,
utterly devoid of trees.
Short grasses held hues of color.
Gazing from afar,
it was like autumn colors in summer.
Returning to the front of the hall,
I gazed afar at the Southern Terrace.
It too had no trees.
Its peak stood alone in elegance,
connecting with the azure sky,
transcendently rising beyond the multitude of peaks.
The Western Terrace, separated by the Central Terrace,
could not be seen.
Before the Bodhisattva Hall,
at the cliff's edge, there is a three-bay pavilion.
Planks are laid on the ground,
with high railings on all four sides.
Below the pavilion is a perilously steep cliff, a thousand ren deep.
An elder monk said:
"In the past, the Tripitaka Master Língxiān of Japan
in this pavilion
beheld ten thousand Bodhisattvas.
After paying homage to them all,
he went to the Pavilion Monastery and met the Abbot Xuánliàng.
From the fourth month, he began lecturing on the Lotus Sutra,
along with the Tiāntāi commentary.
The audience numbered over forty people.
All were disciples of the Venerable Master Yuǎn.
In the morning session at the Pavilion Monastery, he lectured on the Lotus Sutra;
in the evening session at the Nirvana Monastery, he lectured on the 'Stopping and Contemplation.'
The assemblies of the two monasteries
alternated in attending the lectures.
Many also came to listen from other monasteries.
The Chief Monk of the temple, Hóngjī,
together with the Venerable Master Yuǎn, jointly decided
to invite the two abbots
to give these two lecture series.
Truly, it can be said that the Great Huáyán Monastery of Wǔtái Mountain is of the Tiāntāi lineage."
Together with the assembly of monks, I ascended the pavilion,
paying homage to the merits.
The adornments inside and outside the pavilion,
and all the precious objects,
were similar to those of the Bodhisattva Hall.
I saw the parietal bone of a Pratyekabuddha.
Its color was a dull white,
resembling the lightweight stone of our country.
The bone itself was solid and firm,
about the size of two shēng measures.
It was seen to be the bone from above the forehead.
White hairs grew upon it,
about five fen long,
as if having been shaved and regrown.
It was brought by a monk from the Western Regions during the Zhēnguàn era.
There was also a Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript of the Lotus Sutra,
and furthermore, Buddha's relics,
placed inside a glass bottle.
A gold-character Lotus Sutra,
a small-character Lotus Sutra,
were exquisitely refined to the utmost.
Before the pavilion stands a pagoda,
two stories, octagonal,
ornamented with splendid pearls.
At its base is installed an Aśoka Pagoda,
buried underground,
not permitted to be seen by people.
It is one of the eighty-four thousand pagodas built by King Aśoka.
Next, I entered the Shànzhù Pavilion Monastery to rejoice in the merits.
There were over fifty meditation monks,
all wearing coarse woolen robes and carrying khakkhara staffs,
each having come from various regions on pilgrimage.
An imperial decree established it as a temple for protecting the state.
There was a monk of the Tiāntāi school
lecturing on the Four-Part Vinaya,
also a disciple of the Venerable Master Yuǎn.
On the eighteenth day, I attended the invitation from the abbot of the Shànzhù Pavilion Monastery.
Upon arriving there, I broke my fast.
There, I also saw the documents brought from the Guóqīng Temple in Tāizhōu.
Earlier, in Chǔzhōu,
they had been entrusted to the visiting monk Yuánzài Shàngrén.
These were the thirty unresolved articles sent to the Enryaku Temple on Mount Tiāntāi.
The seat master Xiū of Guóqīng Temple
had already thoroughly resolved them.
He then requested the official seal of Tāizhōu.
The prefectural governor had already affixed his seal.
Seat master Jìngwén of the Xiūchán Temple prepared a complete copy.
It was sent to Mount Tiāntāi.
To propagate the teachings of the Tiāntāi school among its various virtuous masters,
along with the letter sent to Tiāntāi by the Japanese monk Wúxíng Héshàng.
The Tiāntāi seat master Wáng had already completed the thorough resolution.
The document requesting the prefectural seal.
The critique and approval by the governor of Tāizhōu.
Along with the wording of the official seal.
All were fully transcribed and sent here.
On the twentieth day, we began our circuit of the terraces.
We went westward from Huáyán Temple.
Ascending a slope, we traveled about seven lǐ.
We arrived at Wángzǐ Temple and drank tea.
Heading west, we ascended a slope for about six or seven lǐ.
We reached Wánghuā Temple.
Continuing west, we ascended a slope for over ten lǐ.
We arrived at the Central Terrace.
On the southern face of the terrace,
there was a Rain-Prayer Cloister.
From the cloister, we went upward for about half a lǐ.
We reached the summit of the terrace.
Near the south on the summit,
there were three iron pagodas.
They had neither tiers nor finials and such.
Their form
was entirely like an inverted bell.
Their circumference was about four arm-spans.
The middle pagoda was four-cornered,
about ten zhàng high.
The ones on both sides were round,
both about eight chǐ high.
They were built by Empress Wǔpó
to pacify Wǔtái.
Wǔpó
refers to Empress Zétiān.
North of the iron pagodas,
there was a four-bay hall.
It enshrined Mañjuśrī and Buddha images. From here, one lǐ and a half to the north,
was the center of the terrace summit.
There was a Jade Flower Pond.
Each side was about four zhàng.
It was called the Dragon Pond.
On a small islet in the center of the pond was a small hall.
It enshrined an image of Mañjuśrī, which people called the Dragon Hall.
The pond water was clear and pure,
about three chǐ deep.
From the bank, one could see the sand at the bottom.
It was clean, with no dust or weeds.
The terrace summit was flat and level,
its circumference about a hundred chō or more.
It rose loftily and alone,
as if
the terrace form were round and towering.
From here, one could see the other four terraces: the Western Terrace,
the Northern Terrace,
were somewhat close to the Central Terrace.
Descending the Central Terrace and ascending northward,
was the southern cliff of the Northern Terrace. Also, descending the Central Terrace and ascending westward,
was the eastern cliff of the Western Terrace.
The terrain of these three terraces was close and connected.
The Eastern Terrace and the Southern Terrace
were both about fifty lǐ from the Central Terrace.
The eastern foot of the Central Terrace
had long ridges, high and low,
winding and meandering,
extending south for fifty lǐ.
The land then connected with the northwestern foot of the Southern Terrace.
The northeastern foot of the Northern Terrace
had ridges descending and then ascending again,
long ridges of varying heights,
extending east for over forty lǐ.
It then connected with the western foot of the Eastern Terrace.
Thus, the five terraces rose high and prominent above the surrounding ridges.
The circumference of the five terraces was five hundred lǐ.
Beyond them were high peaks,
rising high across valleys,
encircling the five terraces like a wall.
The peaks were uneven,
with lush and dense trees.
Only the five summits and the upper halves of their slopes
had no trees.
Now, the Central Terrace
was the center of the four terraces.
All over the terrace, water welled up from the ground.
Soft grass grew over an inch long,
dense and lush,
covering the ground as it grew.
Stepping on it, it lay flat;
lifting the foot, it sprang back up.
With each step, it was wet with water,
cold as ice.
Everywhere there were small depressions,
all filled with water.
All over the terrace were sand and stones,
interspersed with countless stone pagodas.
Fine, soft grass grew among mosses and creepers.
Although the ground was wet with water,
there was no muddy sludge.
Because the mosses and soft grass had dense, spreading roots,
they did not allow travelers to dirty their shoes and feet.
Strange flowers of unusual colors
bloomed all over the mountains.
From the valleys to the summits,
all sides were covered with flowers,
as if spread with brocade.
Their fragrance was rich and pervasive,
permeating people's clothes.
People said
that now, in this fifth month, it was still cold,
and the flowers were not yet in full bloom.
In the sixth and seventh months,
the flowers would bloom even more profusely.
Looking at the colors of these flowers,
they were not found in the human world.
East from the terrace summit,
descending a slope for about half a lǐ,
there was a Bodhisattva Temple.
In summer, it had congee and meals,
provided only for monks and laypeople touring the terraces.
From in front of the iron pagodas, we gradually descended westward.
Traveling over ten lǐ,
we descended a steep slope for about two lǐ.
Then ascending a slope westward for about half a lǐ,
we arrived at the Offering Cloister of the Western Terrace.
Behind the cloister were three large rocky peaks,
precipitous, steep, straight, and elegant.
The three peaks rose together,
named Xiāngshān.
In the past, a monk from India came
and, seeing these three peaks, said,
"I long dwelt at Xiāngshān in the Western Lands.
Now coming here, I see Xiāngshān again.
Has it appeared here early?"
From the Offering Cloister,
ascending westward for five or six lǐ,
we reached the summit of the Western Terrace.
The terrace summit was flat and level,
its circumference about ten chō.
The terrace body was narrow north-south
and broad east-west. Looking east-west,
it was narrow in the east and broad in the west. At the center of the terrace summit,
there was also a Dragon Pond.
Each side was about five zhàng.
In the center of the pond,
was a four-bay Dragon Hall enshrining an image of Mañjuśrī.
Southeast of the pond,
there was a foundation of an iron pagoda built by Empress Zétiān.
It was round and without tiers,
about five chǐ high,
and about two zhàng in circumference.
Mosses, soft grass, and coiled rocks,
stone pagodas strange and unusual,
flowers and plants no different from the Central Terrace.
Water welled up from the ground,
collecting hidden beneath the grass.
In depressions, water pooled.
On three sides, the cliffs were steep,
while the eastern bank meandered gradually down, connecting with the foot of the Central Terrace.
Descending from the western side of the terrace for five or six lǐ,
near a valley was the place where Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti conversed. Two large rocks stood opposite each other, rising high.
One south, one north,
each about three zhàng high.
The tops of the rocks were both flat.
Both had large stone seats.
Tradition says
this was where Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva
met and conversed with Vimalakīrti.
Between the two seats, on a lower rock, were lion hoof prints,
impressed into the stone surface,
about an inch deep.
In front of the rocks was a six-bay tower,
built facing east.
At the southern end was placed an image of Mañjuśrī,
riding a pair of lions.
At the eastern end was placed an image of Vimalakīrti,
sitting on a four-cornered seat. The old man's white
hair on the crown was tied in two knots.
His beard was plain white,
and hung forward,
as if wearing lotus leaves.
He wore a yellow-red robe and a white skirt, over which was draped a fur coat,
the fur mottled with red, white, and black.
His two hands were not in the fur sleeves. His right knee was bent,
placed on the seat.
His left knee was raised upright,
and planted on the seat.
His right elbow rested on a table,
palm up with fingers extended.
His left hand held a fly-whisk,
resting the wrist on his left knee.
His mouth was open, teeth visible,
in a likeness as if speaking or smiling.
Near the front of the seat,
on the west side was a heavenly maiden.
On the east side was a bodhisattva,
holding a bowl full of rice, standing.
Also, in front of this tower,
there was another six-bay tower opposite.
People said
it was built according to the appearance seen during a miraculous manifestation.
A hundred paces or so east from the tower,
was the Pond of Eight Merits.
Water welled up from beneath a large rock.
We toured and viewed until night,
then returned to the Offering Cloister to lodge.
On the twenty-first day, after the morning meal,
we returned to the Bodhisattva Temple on Central Terrace to have tea.
Looking northeast into the distance,
deep in the valley, several dozen chō away,
we saw a silvery-white color.
People said
it was thousand-year-old ice,
for the snow never melts year after year,
accumulating into ice.
The valley is deep and shaded, blocked by the cliffs ahead so that sunlight never reaches it.
Therefore, since ancient times,
not a speck of snow has ever melted there.
The ridge in front of the valley
is precisely the eastern foot of Central Terrace.
From the Bodhisattva Temple, we went north along the eastern bank of Central Terrace,
descending a winding slope for about ten lǐ,
then ascended another slope for over ten lǐ,
arriving at North Terrace.
The summit of the terrace is roughly six chō in circumference.
The terrace itself is rounded.
At the southern end of the summit is a Dragon Hall.
Inside the hall is a pond,
its water deep and dark,
filling the hall with a clear pool.
The hall is divided into three sections:
the middle is the Dragon King’s palace,
with a statue of the Dragon King placed beside the pond.
A bridge is built over the pond,
leading across to the front of the Dragon King’s seat.
This is the king
of the five hundred poisonous dragons of the Five Terraces,
each terrace having one hundred poisonous dragons.
All of them
take this Dragon King as their lord.
This Dragon King and his subjects
were subdued by Mañjuśrī
and took refuge, not daring to commit evil.
To the left and right of the Dragon Palace,
separated by a wooden wall,
are statues of Mañjuśrī.
In front of the Dragon Hall,
there is a support monastery.
We saw a monk there
who had not eaten for three years,
taking only one meal a day,
consuming mud and earth as his fast.
He made a vow for three years
not to descend from the terrace summit.
There are several disciple cloisters.
The front cloister overlooks a deep valley,
with steep cliffs on the terrace,
reaching perhaps a thousand rèn.
This valley is where Mañjuśrī once manifested a golden bell and jeweled tower.
It is now called Bell Tower Valley.
The western source of the valley
is at the base of the eastern bank of Central Terrace.
South of the valley is a high ridge.
The northern bank of the ridge is extremely perilous,
descending deep into the valley where the thousand-year-old ice
gleams brightly in the hidden depths.
Looking southeast again,
we saw the Great Huáyán Temple.
At the center of the terrace summit,
there is an iron pagoda from Empress Wǔ Zétiān’s era,
surrounded by many stone pagodas.
Soft grass, strawberries, and moss
cover the ground everywhere.
Every three or four steps,
there are countless small wells and ponds,
called Dragon Ponds.
Water bubbles up from the sandy bottom, clear and shallow.
The northern and eastern banks are steep and high,
overlooking deep valleys.
The northern valley is called Sòng Valley.
Once, a monk following the Tiāntāi master Zhìzhě
practiced the Lotus Sūtra Samādhi,
performing rituals and repentance,
and there he beheld the bodhisattva Samantabhadra and the Many-Jeweled Pagoda.
Although the southern side is a perilous path,
there is a route one can climb.
The northwestern bank gradually slopes down like a curtain,
eventually becoming a deep valley.
At the eastern end of the terrace summit is a high mound,
called the Arhat Terrace.
Across the terrace, there are also no trees.
From the Arhat Terrace,
descending southeast,
along the path, there are many scorched stones covering the ground.
There is the semblance of a stone wall in a square shape,
filled with scorched stones inside.
This is where a hell was manifested.
In the past,
the prefect of Dàizhōu
was violent by nature
and did not believe in cause and effect.
Hearing of hell, he did not believe it.
While touring and admiring the terraces, gazing around,
he came to this place
and angrily saw fierce flames
burning the rocks,
with black smoke soaring into the sky.
The fire and embers blazed brilliantly,
forming a surrounding corridor.
Hell guards appeared before him, wrathful and sorrowful.
The prefect was terrified
and took refuge in the great sage Mañjuśrī.
The fierce flames immediately vanished.
Their traces remain visible today:
scorched stones piled into a wall,
roughly five zhàng in circumference,
filled with black stones inside.
On the twenty-second day,
after congee, we went along the eastern flank of North Terrace, descending northeast on a winding slope,
following the ridge east for about twenty lǐ,
arriving at Shàngmǐ Pǔtōngyuàn.
In the hall, we suddenly saw five beams of light
directly enter the hall, illuminating it,
then suddenly vanish.
Wéizhèng,
Wéixiǎo, and others
were together in the hall
and all said
they saw nothing.
We marveled endlessly at this.
After the morning meal,
we followed the ridge eastward,
gradually ascending a slope for twenty lǐ,
and arrived at East Terrace.
At the eastern end of the terrace is a support monastery.
We entered the monastery to have tea.
Ascending southward up a slope for about two lǐ,
we reached the terrace summit.
There is a three-bay hall,
built with piled stones as walls,
each side roughly five zhàng,
and about one zhàng high.
Inside the hall is enshrined a statue of Mañjuśrī.
Near the northwest of the hall are three iron pagodas from Empress Wǔ Zétiān’s era,
their form the same as those on the other terraces.
On the summit, there is no dragon pond,
nor any water on the ground.
The grass grows somewhat thick.
The summit’s circumference
is about ten zhàng on each side.
The terrace itself is longer north-south,
narrower east-west.
The northern base extends for about one lǐ.
South of the terrace is a ridge,
undulating and stretching for about three lǐ.
Yet the terrace summit is the highest and most prominent,
with no trees.
From the summit, descending directly east for half a lǐ,
on a steep cliff, there is a cave,
called the Nārayaṇa Cave.
People say
that in the past, the Buddha Nārayaṇa
practiced the path in this cave,
then departed westward.
Inside the cave, it is damp,
with water dripping at the entrance.
It is six chǐ wide.
Inside the cave, it is dark,
likely with dragons hidden within.
As evening approached,
we returned to the support monastery to lodge.
Just as dusk was about to fall,
the sky suddenly turned overcast.
In the eastern valley bottom,
white clouds gathered densely,
suddenly red, suddenly white, swirling and flying.
Thunder rumbled,
echoing tumultuously in the deep valley.
We stood on the high summit, watching:
wind, rain, and hail fell chaotically together.
Late into the night, it ceased.
On the twenty-third day, after the morning meal, I descended from the platform.
I then returned to the Upper Mi Pǔtōng Temple.
I proceeded directly south down the slope.
After traveling about eighteen lǐ, I entered a valley.
I then went southeast for three or four lǐ.
Then, I traveled west into the valley for about one lǐ.
I arrived at the Vajra Cave.
The cave is located at the edge of the valley.
The monk from the Western Regions, Fótuóbōlì, came empty-handed.
He arrived at the mountain gate.
Mañjuśrī manifested a human form and did not permit him to enter the mountain.
Instead, he instructed him to go to the Western Regions to fetch the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa Vijaya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
That monk then returned to the Western Heaven.
He fetched the scripture and came to this mountain.
Mañjuśrī received and guided him.
Together they entered this cave.
As soon as Bōlì entered,
the cave door closed by itself.
To this day, it has not opened.
The cave rock is hard, dense, and tinged with yellow. Facing the cave entrance, there is a tall tower.
The cave entrance is below the tower.
People cannot see it.
To the east of the tower,
there is a support monastery.
Above the tower at the cave entrance,
there is a revolving scripture repository.
It is hexagonal in construction.
This is seen in the cave records.
Inside the cave, there are many sacred traces from the Western Heaven. During the time of Buddha Vipaśyin,
the great immortal Mólì of the Fragrant Mountain
made three thousand kinds of seven-jeweled musical instruments.
After that Buddha's nirvana,
Mañjuśrī
brought them
into this cave. During the time of Buddha Krakucchanda,
the Heaven King of Tuṣita made a bell.
It could hold one hundred and twenty shí.
Those who heard its sound
might attain the four fruits [of śrāvakas]
or reach the first ground [of bodhisattvas], and so on.
After the Buddha's nirvana,
Mañjuśrī
brought this bell
and placed it in this cave. During the time of Buddha Kāśyapa,
a silver konghou was made.
It had eighty-four thousand melodies.
Eighty-four thousand melodies,
each addressing one affliction.
After the Buddha's parinirvana,
Mañjuśrī
brought this konghou
and stored it in the cave.
A jeweled pagoda containing the whole body relic of the second Buddha of the Constellation Kalpa, with one thousand three hundred levels,
was brought by Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī
and stored in this cave.
Silver paper with golden script from the Land of Zhèndàn,
and writings from the hundred koṭis of four-continent worlds,
were collected by Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī
and stored in this cave.
Going up the slope about a hundred paces from the cave,
there is a Mañjuśrī Hall.
A Samantabhadra Hall.
This is the place where the Great Monk Dàchāo
saw the golden-colored world.
As the day grew late,
I returned to the Dàhuāyán Gāngwéi Temple.
I was led to the Nirvana Courtyard and settled in a room below the pavilion.
This was the room of the Venerable Xuánliàng,
the lecturer on the *Lotus Sutra*.
The lecturer, due to his lectures,
is temporarily residing in the pavilion courtyard of the Venerable Yuǎn and the lecturer Wénjiàn's courtyard.
The texts of the Tiāntāi teachings are fully available here.
On the twenty-third day, I began copying Tiāntāi texts not yet available in Japan.
On the sixth day of the sixth month,
imperial envoys arrived.
In the temple,
all the monks came out to welcome and receive them.
It is the annual custom
for the emperor to send robes, alms bowls, incense, flowers, and so forth.
The envoys deliver them to the mountain to be distributed to the twelve great monasteries.
Five hundred fine silk vestments,
five hundred bales of silk floss,
one thousand bolts of cloth for kasayas,
dyed blue-green,
one thousand liang of incense,
one thousand jin of tea,
one thousand hand towels.
Additionally, by imperial order, they make offerings and tour the twelve great monasteries to provide vegetarian feasts.
On the seventh day, an imperial vegetarian feast was held at this temple.
After the feast,
the entire *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was recited.
In the evening,
the imperial envoys, along with several tens of monks,
ascended to the Bodhisattva Hall seeking manifestations.
They went to the Nirvana Courtyard
to pay respects to the Venerable Yuǎn.
On the eighth day, the imperial envoys provided a vegetarian feast for one thousand monks.
On the ninth day, after the morning meal,
the imperial envoys went to the Jīngé Temple.
On the eleventh day, the present emperor's birthday,
an imperial order was given to all the monasteries on Wǔtái Mountain
to hold birthday vegetarian feasts.
All the monasteries rang their bells simultaneously.
The most senior elders, five or six in number,
rose from their seats to offer incense.
I heard the imperial envoys offered incense at the Jīngé Temple and then returned to the capital.
On the twenty-first day, the weather was beautifully clear.
The sky was azure blue,
without a single cloud.
Together with Wéizhèng,
Wéixiǎo,
and several monks from the courtyard,
in the front courtyard of the courtyard pavilion,
we saw colored light clouds.
The light was radiant and brilliant,
its colors exceptionally beautiful.
It shone brightly, flowing through the sky,
right above our heads,
for a long time before disappearing.
Several tens of monks in the courtyard
who did not come out
did not get to see it.
There was a mendicant monk from Fénzhōu,
who for ten years
had made offerings to the twelve monasteries of Wǔtái
and all the common hermitages.
His name was Yìyuán.
As he was delivering this year's offerings,
he also witnessed this auspicious light.
With tears in his eyes, he said,
"Since Yìyuán first resolved to do this ten years ago,
I have delivered offerings throughout the mountain every year without fail.
I have never witnessed a single sign.
Now, together with a foreign Tripiṭaka Master,
I have seen the light clouds.
I truly understand that although our places of birth are in different lands,
receiving the great sage's transformation shows we share a karmic connection.
From now on, let us forge a karmic bond together,
forever becoming members of Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī's retinue."
On the twenty-ninth day,
I finished copying the Tiāntāi teachings.
I made a catalog
and presented it to the Venerable Yuǎn,
asking him to inscribe his dharma name.
First day of the seventh month.
Preparing for the journey to Cháng'ān.
Arranging the luggage.
Heard people say
that from Wǔtái to Cháng'ān,
heading southwest,
it is over two thousand lǐ
to reach Cháng'ān.
Before the morning meal,
paid respects to the senior monk Yuǎn
and the two abbots who lecture on the Tiāntāi texts of Zhǐguān and Wénjù,
as well as the entire assembly.
The monastery head monk Guǎngchū
offered a simple farewell meal.
After the meal, we departed.
The entire monastery assembly saw us off
to outside the main gate.
We wiped away tears and clasped hands in farewell.
Took the Bamboo Forest Road.
Passing in front of the Zhúlín Temple,
headed southwest,
crossed over a high ridge,
and stayed overnight at the Jiāngù Púsà Courtyard of the Bǎomó Zhènguó Jīngé Temple.
The chief alms-gathering monk of all the terraces, Yìyuán,
was also returning to Fénzhōu.
Today, from the Huāyán Temple,
he caught up and stayed in the same courtyard.
The courtyard monks served tea and said:
"The Tripitaka Master Língxiān of Japan
formerly resided in this courtyard for two years.
Afterwards, he moved to the Qīfó Jiàojiè Courtyard and passed away.
That Tripitaka Master
himself peeled skin from his hand, four cùn long and three cùn wide,
painted a Buddha image on it,
and enshrined it in a gilt-bronze pagoda he made.
It is now present below the golden pavilion of this temple,
receiving perpetual offerings."
Second day.
Together with chief alms-giver Yìyuán and several monks from the temple,
opened the Golden Pavilion.
Worshipped the sacred image of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva riding a blue-maned lion.
Golden-colored countenance,
solemn and dignified beyond compare.
Also saw the holy man Língxiān's
hand-skin Buddha image and the gilt-bronze pagoda.
Also saw a Pratyekabuddha's tooth,
and flesh-body relics of the Buddha.
Above the Bodhisattva's head hung a seven-jeweled canopy,
an item bestowed by imperial decree.
The pavilion has nine bays and three stories,
over one hundred chǐ high.
Walls, eaves, rafters, pillars—
nowhere is unpainted.
Adorned inside and out
with all the world's rare treasures.
Majestically rising alone above the fir forest.
White clouds drift peacefully below, dense and layered.
The azure stories tower aloft, lofty and prominent.
Next, ascended to the second story.
Worshipped the five Buddha images of the Vajraśekhara Yoga.
These were made by Tripitaka Master Bùkōng
for the state.
Modeled after the style of the Nālandā Temple in India.
Each Buddha has two attendant bodhisattvas,
all arranged on a wooden altar.
Next, climbed to the third story.
Worshipped the gilt images of the five Buddhas of the Cakravartin Yoga assembly.
Each Buddha has one attendant bodhisattva.
Two bodhisattvas are in a joined-palms posture,
standing in front of the Buddha, facing south.
The mudras and appearances of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas
differ from those on the second story.
On the plastered inner walls,
are painted various deity maṇḍalas.
The coloring is not yet finished.
These were also made by Tripitaka Master Bùkōng for the state.
After viewing and worshipping,
descended from the pavilion to the Samantabhadra practice site.
Saw the scripture repository pavilion.
The Great Canon of over six thousand scrolls
are all on dark blue paper with gold and silver characters,
with sandalwood and jade ivory rollers.
Looking at the donor's inscription,
it says Zhèng Dàojié,
a man of Cháng'ān.
On the fourteenth day of the fifth month of the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era,
while touring Wǔtái,
he personally saw the Great Sage and ten thousand bodhisattvas and a golden-colored world.
Thus he vowed
to transcribe the Great Canon in gold and silver characters, six thousand scrolls.
There is also a painted footprint with the thousand-spoked wheel mark,
and an accompanying written explanation stating:
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Emperor Tàizōng sent an envoy with a robe to India.
He saw an ancient temple of King Aśoka,
where on a stone was a Buddha's footprint,
one chǐ eight cùn long,
six cùn wide.
He obtained a rubbing of the Buddha's footprint
and brought it to the capital city.
It was then copied and transferred here for enshrinement.
Next, opened the Dhāraṇī Maṇḍala practice site.
Worshipped the honored images.
This was the altar of Hánguāng,
a disciple of Tripitaka Master Bùkōng,
who, to ensure the long-lasting prosperity of the Lǐ family's reign,
received an imperial decree to perform dhāraṇī recitation.
The altar surface is three cubits,
made by mixing white sandalwood juice with clay.
Whenever the wind blows,
the fragrance carries far.
There are many gilt-bronze ritual implements,
all placed on the altar.
Next, opened the Samantabhadra Hall.
Worshipped the image of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Three horses stand side by side,
with one bodhisattva image placed on their backs.
The hall's interior and exterior adornments,
the painted colors and carved designs,
cannot be fully described.
Seven-jeweled scripture boxes,
pearl-embroidered Buddhas—
using threads to string pearls
and embroider them onto silk.
The craftsmanship is wondrous.
As for the remaining objects,
there is no leisure to record them all.
After worshipping and viewing,
returned to the courtyard for the midday meal.
After the meal,
together with chief alms-giver, the ascetic monk Yìyuán, and several others,
formed a single group
and headed for the Southern Terrace.
West of the Jīngé Temple,
five lǐ from the temple,
there is the Qīngliáng Temple.
It now administers the Southern Terrace.
This Wǔtái Mountain
is collectively called Qīngliáng Mountain.
Among the temples built in the mountains,
this temple was the very first,
hence named Qīngliáng Temple.
In the temple is the Qīngliáng Stone.
Led by the ascetic,
we headed for the Southern Terrace,
so could not reach that temple.
Exited the main gate of the Jīngé Temple,
followed the ridge southward,
climbed a slope for twenty lǐ,
reached the western end of the Southern Terrace.
Turned east,
walked along the southern edge of the terrace
for four or five lǐ,
and arrived on the terrace.
There are no trees at all.
On the southeastern side of the terrace,
there is an offering courtyard.
From the courtyard, heading north,
climbed a slope about three hundred paces,
and finally reached the terrace summit.
In a three-bay hall,
is enshrined an image of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
made of white jade stone,
riding a white jade lion.
Soft grasses grow thick and lush,
scattered fragrant flowers
pervade the terrace with fragrance.
The body of the terrace, northwest and southeast,
has long ridges, high and low,
winding and gradually receding.
The eastern, northern, and western sides
are steep cliffs overlooking deep valleys.
Standing at the summit facing north,
the other four terraces are distantly visible,
clearly before the eyes.
Turning around to survey all around, the five summits are rounded and high,
transcendently beautiful above all other peaks.
A thousand peaks, a hundred ridges,
with pines and firs lush and dense,
irregularly interspersed below the five summits.
Deep gorges and profound valleys, their bottoms unseen.
Secluded springs and mountain stream waters—
only the sound of flowing is heard.
Rare birds soar among the multitude of peaks,
their wings reaching great heights,
but few fly onto the terrace summit.
The land of the five summits—
for five hundred lǐ around,
on all four sides, high peaks stand arrayed,
encircling and embracing Wǔtái,
stretching perhaps a thousand lǐ.
All their sharp ridges
form a layered fortress encircling it.
Peaks and valleys, layer upon layer,
who knows how many layers.
Moreover, entering the Táishān from the east,
traveling through mountain valleys,
for five hundred lǐ,
climbing to the tops of jagged cliffs,
descending to the bottoms of deep valleys.
On the eleventh day, we set out at dawn.
After traveling about twenty li,
we arrived at Dàgàn Pǔtōngyuàn to break our fast at midday.
Traveling another twenty-five li,
we reached Tàdìdiàn to spend the night.
On the twelfth day, we set out during the fifth watch.
After traveling thirty-five li,
we arrived at Báiyáng Pǔtōngyuàn to break our fast at midday.
Traveling another fifteen li,
we reached Sānjiāo Yì to rest.
Next, we entered the estate of Dìngjué Sì.
We saw a water-powered mill,
named the Sānjiāo Mill.
Traveling another fifteen li,
we arrived at Gǔchéng Pǔtōngyuàn to spend the night.
On the thirteenth day,
we set out at daybreak.
After traveling fifteen li, we reached Tàiyuán Fǔ.
It belongs to Hédōng Dào.
This is Běijīng.
It is about two thousand li from Xījīng.
Entering through the north gate, we stayed at Huáyán Xiàsì.
We met the South Indian monk Fǎdá.
He had previously come from Táishān.
He said of himself,
"I am a third-generation descendant of the Tripiṭaka Master Jiūmóluóshí.
I am a monk of Dàzhuāngyán Sì on Wǔtái Shān.
Those who descend the mountain
all stay at this temple below,
hence it is called Huáyán Xiàsì."
The patron Yìyuán Tóutuó
led us to this temple.
Tóutuó had been our companion since Táishān.
Along the entire journey, he managed the porridge, rice, and tea,
never lacking anything.
On the fifteenth day, we accepted the invitation of the temple master of Sìzhòng Sì.
Together with Tóutuó and others,
we went to that temple for the midday meal.
After the meal, we entered Dùtuō Sì
to pay respects at the Ullambana assembly.
Then we entered the prefecture to see Lóngquán,
and next entered Chóngfú Sì.
We paid respects at the Buddha hall, the pavilion below, and the various courtyards.
All were adorned and arrayed,
their brilliance dazzling to the eye.
Offerings were displayed, precious and marvelous.
The entire city's people came to pay their respects.
In the evening, they performed the ceremony of self-purification.
On the sixteenth day, we entered Kāiyuán Sì.
We ascended the pavilion to gaze out.
Inside the pavilion was a statue of Maitreya Buddha,
cast in iron,
the gilded Buddha body over three zhang tall,
seated upon a jeweled throne.
The decorations in each temple
each excelled in their own way.
On the seventeenth day,
we accepted the invitation of the Jiedushi's fellow officer Hú.
Together with the patron monk Yìyuán,
we went to his residence for the midday meal.
The Ullambana assemblies at the various temples
began on the fifteenth day
and concluded on the seventeenth.
On the eighteenth day, at the side of the South Indian Tripiṭaka Master Fǎdá,
we copied the stele inscriptions and other records of the various spiritual manifestations on Wǔtái Shān.
On the eighteenth day, we intended to depart for Cháng'ān.
The ascetic monk Yìyuán
hired a master craftsman
and personally provided a piece of silk fabric
to paint a picture of the manifestations on Wǔtái Shān,
intending to send it to Japan.
Because we were waiting for the painting to be completed,
we could not depart.
On the nineteenth day, accompanying Tóutuó,
we accepted the invitation of the female disciple Zhēnrúxìng.
We went to her residence to break our fast at midday.
As she had accompanied us on the pilgrimage to Táishān,
she was now our host.
On the twenty-second day, together with Tóutuó, we went to the residence of the nun Zhēnrúxīn for the midday meal.
She was also one who had accompanied us on the pilgrimage to Wǔtái Shān.
On the twenty-third day, together with Tóutuó, we went to the residence of the Vinaya master at Dàyè Sì for the midday meal.
There were three nuns who were great masters,
who had also accompanied Tóutuó
on the pilgrimage to Táishān.
On the 26th, the painting of the manifestation scene was completed.
The ascetic said:
"I am delighted to have met the Tripitaka Master from Japan.
We toured the terrace together.
We witnessed the great sage's manifestation together.
Now, I have painted one scroll depicting the manifestation scene and respectfully present it to you.
Please take it back to Japan for veneration.
May those who view it with reverence arouse the aspiration for enlightenment.
May those with karmic affinity form connections through it.
May we all be reborn together in the great assembly of Mañjuśrī."
After the midday meal, we bid farewell to all the monks in the monastery.
We then began our journey toward Cháng'ān.
The ascetic said:
"My original intention
was to escort the Reverend
all the way to Fénzhōu,
acting as host along the road.
But now that I have arrived here,
some matters I must attend to are not yet finished.
I unavoidably must stay for ten-some days.
Thus, I cannot fulfill my original request."
The monk Lìng Yǎ, who toured the terrace with us, said:
"I wish to be able to escort the Reverend
to Cháng'ān."
The ascetic instructed him, saying:
"Act diligently on my behalf to manage affairs.
Exert effort with the luggage.
Serve attentively; do not let the distant guest feel lonely on the road."
Then we set off together.
The ascetic said:
"I will accompany you out of the city,
and we will go together to pay homage to the Western Mountains."
So we exited together through the city's west gate.
Traveling westward for three or four *li*,
we reached a stone mountain,
named Jìn Mountain.
The entire mountain has coal.
People from near and far, from all the surrounding prefectures, come to take it for burning,
for cooking food.
It has an extremely strong fiery nature.
It appears as if the rocky cliffs have been charred and transformed into coal.
People say:
"It was burned by heavenly fire."
I privately think:
That is not necessarily so.
This is rather the result of the collective karma of sentient beings.
At the mountain entrance, there is a small temple,
named Shímén Temple.
In the temple, there is a monk
who has been reciting the *Lotus Sutra* for many years.
Recently, he miraculously obtained *śarīra* relics.
It was seen that the entire city's people all came to make offerings.
Monks and laypeople filled the temple,
their number beyond count.
The original source of obtaining the *śarīra* was this:
The sutra-reciting monk, at night in his room,
was sitting and reciting the sutra.
Three beams of radiant light came and illuminated,
filling the room with brightness,
and shining throughout the temple.
Seeking the source of the light,
it came from west of the temple,
emerging from the base of a cliff.
Every night it illuminated the room and the temple grounds.
Several days later,
that monk traced the light to the cliff site.
Digging into the ground over ten feet deep,
he obtained three vases of Buddha's *śarīra*.
In a blue glass vase were seven grains of *śarīra*.
In a white glass vase,
were five grains of *śarīra*.
Within a golden vase,
were three grains of *śarīra*.
He brought them and placed them in the Buddha hall for veneration.
From Tàiyuán city and the various villages,
noble and common, men and women,
as well as all the prefectural officials, high and low, all came
to bow in reverence and make offerings.
Everyone said:
"This is due to the Reverend's upholding of the *Lotus Sutra*,
an inconceivable power miraculously obtained."
From the city to the mountain,
people coming and going filled the road.
Dense and crowded, they viewed the relics, marveling at them.
From Shímén Temple, we went west up a slope.
Traveling about two *li*,
we reached Tóngzǐ Temple.
This is the place where Master Cí'ēn Terrace,
avoiding the Silla monk Master Xuán Cè,
came from Cháng'ān
and first lectured on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only).
In the two-story hall,
the entire hall contained a large Buddha image.
We saw a stele,
the text of which said:
"In the past, Meditation Master Lǐ from Jìzhōu
came to dwell on this mountain.
Suddenly he saw a five-colored radiant cloud
rising from the ground into the sky, shining everywhere.
Within that radiant cloud,
there were four youths
sitting on blue lotus seats, playing.
A sound shook the great earth.
Cliffs and peaks crumbled and fell.
At the place on the bank that collapsed,
an image of Amitābha Buddha appeared.
All of Sān Jìn came to pay respects.
There were many spiritual wonders.
The Meditation Master fully recorded and reported it,
requesting to build a temple.
Subsequently, this temple was constructed.
Based on this original auspicious sign,
it was named Tóngzǐ Temple (Youth Temple).
Respectfully, an Amitābha Buddha image was carved.
The appearing countenance was majestic, pure as jade, dignified and beautiful; the seated body
was seventeen *zhàng* high,
and one hundred *chǐ* wide.
Guānyīn and Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
each were twelve *zhàng*."
On the 27th, after gruel, we departed.
Here, we parted with the offering host, the ascetic Yì Yuán.
Together with the monk Lìng Yǎ, who toured the terrace with us,
we formed one traveling party,
heading together toward the Western Capital.
From Tóngzǐ Temple,
we crossed a ridge to the south,
and reached Yǔhuā Temple for the midday meal.
From Yǔhuā Temple, heading southwest,
we exited the mountains and traveled forty *li*,
reaching Qīngliáng County.
We entered Pǔtōng Lodge to stay overnight.
The lodge master did not understand the etiquette for hosting guests.
On the 28th, we traveled southwest for fifteen *li*,
reaching a house in Jìn Village for the midday meal.
Traveling southwest for twenty-five *li*,
we reached Shígāo Village.
We entered Shítái Lodge to stay overnight.
On the 29th, traveling southwest for twenty-five *li*,
we reached a Lǐ family in Wénshuǐ County for the midday meal.
This was a direct disciple of the ascetic Yì Yuán.
The food was proper.
After the meal, we traveled forty *li*,
reaching Guōzhà Village.
We entered the village temple to stay overnight.
The lodge master monk
was displeased to see guests.
On the first day of the eighth month,
traveling southwest for twenty-five *li*,
we reached Dòngzhòngxiāng Temple in Fénzhōu for the midday meal.
East of the temple is the Fén River's still water.
The Fén River flows here and forms a still expanse,
hence it is called a 'still water' (bó).
It is about a thousand *tǐng* in circumference.
Then it gradually flows southward,
reaching Hézhōng Prefecture,
and enters the Yellow River.
From Dòngzhòngxiāng Temple,
traveling west for five *li*,
we reached the south-facing gate on the west side of Fénzhōu's city wall.
We entered Fǎjīn Temple, Nièpán Lodge, to stay overnight.
This lodge belongs to the Táishān offering host, the ascetic Yì Yuán.
In Tàiyuán, he earnestly requested, saying:
"When you reach Fénzhōu, you must come to the lodge to rest."
Therefore, we came to the lodge to stay.
The prefectural officer, surnamed Hé,
came to the temple
to visit and ensure our well-being.
He is a disciple of the ascetic Yì Yuán.
Seeing this distant guest,
he acted as host with great attentiveness.
West from the prefecture,
fifty *li* from the temple,
in the mountains is Guǎngchéng Lodge.
There is the Preceptor Xiān Wù,
who lectures on the Tiāntāi *Zhǐguān* (Calming and Contemplation).
He has over fifty disciples.
He is currently in the prefecture.
Eighty *li* south of the prefecture,
there is Bǎofú Mountain, lofty and steep.
People say:
It is the place where King of Emptiness Buddha practiced the Way.
To this day, there are many sacred traces.
On the nineteenth day, traveled thirty li south.
Reached the boundary of Jīngzhào Prefecture.
Had the midday meal at Lìyáng County.
At the southern end of the county,
saw the funeral procession for the late emperor returning to the capital city.
This was the envoy for the burial of the late Kāichéng Emperor.
Tents and military troops
were arrayed for five li.
Soldiers stood facing each other on both sides of the main road.
They did not obstruct commoners, horses, carriages, or people passing along the central road.
West of the county, eighty or ninety li away,
there is a tomb mound in the mountains.
It lies over two hundred li east of the capital.
Passed through the military encampment.
Traveled thirty-five li south to the Wèi River Bridge at Gāolíng County.
The river is about one li wide.
The bridge is similarly wide.
The town overlooks the Wèi River.
It is on the northern bank. The Wèi River originally flows out from Tǔfān,
running eastward far into the Yellow River.
Crossed the bridge and traveled five li south.
Arrived at Sānjiādiàn and stayed overnight at the Buddhist hall.
On the twentieth day, early morning, traveled twenty-five li south.
Arrived at Bàqiáodiàn in Wànnián County for the midday meal. The Bà River originally flows from Zhōngnán Mountain,
entering the Wèi River.
After the meal,
from Bà Bridge,
traveled fifteen li south.
Arrived at the Chǎn River Bridge.
The Chǎn River flows from Zhōngnán Mountain,
entering the Wèi River.
The Bà and Chǎn rivers
flow northward.
The water is clear.
Only the Jīng River's source was not yet inquired about.
Traveled ten li west.
Arrived in front of Zhāngjìng Temple east of Cháng'ān city and rested.
The temple is east of the city,
outside Tōnghuà Gate.
From outside Tōnghuà Gate,
traveled about three li south.
Arrived outside Chūnmíng Gate.
Stayed overnight at the West Chan Cloister of Zhènguó Temple.
On the twenty-second day, before noon,
the funeral procession returned.
Entered through Tōnghuà Gate.
After the meal, left Zhènguó Temple.
Entered Chūnmíng Gate.
Went to Dàxīngshàn Temple and stayed overnight at the West Chan Cloister.
On the twenty-third day, after the meal,
went to the Left Street Merit Inspection Office.
Met the Investigating Officer and Censor-in-Attendance in charge of inspections,
surnamed Zhào, named Liàn.
Submitted a petition,
requesting permission to lodge in the city's temples to seek a teacher.
The petition text is as follows:
Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén,
disciple monks Wéizhèng,
Wéixiǎo,
lay follower Dīng Xióngwàn,
together with the Qīngzhōu travel permit.
The aforementioned Yuánrén and others,
in the third year of Kāichéng,
followed the tribute envoy to seek and inquire about Buddhism.
This year in March,
obtained the Qīngzhōu travel permit,
entered Wǔtái Mountain,
paid respects and visited the sacred sites.
Then arrived here,
intending to study the sacred Dharma.
Humbly request
permission to lodge in the city's temples,
to seek a teacher and listen to teachings.
Respectfully presented as above.
Humbly await your decision.
The attached document is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
Twenty-third day of the eighth month, fifth year of Kāichéng. Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén, submits.
The Investigating Censor-in-Attendance
assigned an inspection officer,
to lead the monks,
and settle them at Zīshèng Temple.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the hour of chén,
the Inspection Office officer
prepared a document assigning an inspection officer,
ordering an audience with the Merit Commissioner.
The Left Street Merit Commissioner, Imperial Guard General-in-Chief, Palace Attendant with Honors Equal to the Three Excellencies, Administrator of Palace Affairs, Senior General Qiú Shìliáng,
enfeoffed with three thousand households.
The monks followed the inspection officer to the commissioner.
Traveled north from the temple,
passed through four wards and entered Wàngxiān Gate.
Then entered Xuánhuà Gate.
Passed further through the Inner Palace Attendants' Gate,
and the General Supervisory Office,
entered another gate,
arrived at the southern gate of the commissioner's office.
Inside the gate is the Left Divine Strategy Infantry and Cavalry Gate.
Passed through six gates in total,
arrived at the commissioner's office desk and submitted the petition,
requesting a decision.
After detailed questioning about the circumstances,
prepared another petition,
summarizing the relevant matters.
As follows:
Japanese monk Yuánrén,
disciple monks Wéizhèng,
Wéixiǎo,
lay follower Dīng Xióngwàn.
The aforementioned Yuánrén and others,
in the fourth month of the third year of Kāichéng,
followed their country's tribute envoy,
boarded a ship and crossed the sea, arriving.
On the second day of the seventh month,
arrived at Báihú Town, Hǎilíng County, Yángzhōu.
Within the eighth month, arrived in Yángzhōu,
lodged at Kāiyuán Temple.
Spent one winter.
In the second month of the fourth year of Kāichéng,
left Yángzhōu,
arrived in Chǔzhōu,
lodged at Kāiyuán Temple.
By the seventh month,
arrived at Chìshān Monastery, Wéndēng County, Dēngzhōu, and spent one winter.
By the second month of this year,
left Dēngzhōu,
arrived in Qīngzhōu in the third month,
temporarily stayed at Lóngxīng Temple.
After about ten days,
then from Military Governor Shòu Shàngshū,
obtained a travel permit.
On the first day of the fifth month,
arrived at Wǔtái Mountain,
toured and paid respects at the sacred sites.
On the first day of the seventh month,
departed from Wǔtái.
Now, on the twentieth day of the third month,
arrived in the city.
Now request
temporary lodging in the city's temples,
to seek a teacher and listen to teachings,
before returning to our country.
Respectfully presented as above.
Humbly request your decision.
The attached document is as stated above.
Respectfully submitted.
Twenty-fourth day of the eighth month, fifth year of Kāichéng. Japanese monk seeking the Dharma, Yuánrén, submits.
Because the Commissioner with Honors did not appear,
could not present the petition.
The desk officer Hé Pànguān sent us,
to be settled at Nèihùguó Tiānwáng Temple.
The temple is north of the Left Divine Strategy Army polo field.
The temple is separated from the inner palace by a wall,
that is, the northeastern corner of the imperial city's inner wall.
Constantly stationed with fourteen monks to perform chanting.
The monks all around saw the guests.
On the twenty-fifth day, after the meal,
from the commissioner's office, an envoy summoned the monks.
Followed the envoy into the commissioner's office.
Received a document from the Merit Commissioner stating:
Temporarily lodge at Zīshèng Temple.
The temple administrators are ordered to provide for them.
The Investigating Censor-in-Attendance,
in accordance with the commissioner's note, forwarded the note to Zīshèng Temple.
Then assigned an inspection officer
to escort us to the temple,
and temporarily settled us in the pavilion west of the storehouse.
On the twenty-sixth day, rain fell.
Toward evening,
the temple administrators arranged quarters,
settling us in the Pure Land Cloister.
The cloister's head monk, Shī'ān,
is devout,
saw the guest monks,
and inquired with earnest concern.
Often asked various monks,
seeking one who knows the Dharma of mindful recitation.
Had not yet found a definite one.
On the fifth day of the ninth month,
at night, focused mind on Vaiśravaṇa,
vowed and begged to be shown one who knows the Dharma.
Heard that
Yángzhōu Military Governor Lǐ Déyù
had an imperial order to enter the capital.
On the third day of the ninth month,
entered the palace to assume the post of Chief Minister.
On the morning of the sixth day, during the court assembly.
The monk of this monastery, Huáiqìng,
whose profession is recitation and meditation,
brought five grains of Buddha's relics
and had me pay homage.
He said:
"If you wish to master esoteric teachings,
I know of a person within the city who understands the great Dharma.
The monk Rùn of Qīnglóng Temple.
He only understands the Womb Realm,
and has deeply mastered one practice.
Throughout the city, all acknowledge him as a master.
