The rear office of the Lùfǔ Circuit was located on Píngkāng Ward on the left street of the capital.
Jiāng Sūn, the yāyá of the Lùfǔ Circuit.
Managed the affairs of his circuit at the office.
An imperial decree ordered his arrest.
He escaped, and his whereabouts are unknown.
He was sought everywhere but not captured.
Only his wife and children were apprehended.
They were executed, and the family was destroyed.
Someone reported.
That Jiāng Sūn, the rear yāyá of the Lùfǔ Circuit, had shaved his head.
And was now hiding among the monks in the city.
An imperial decree ordered the Commissioners of Merit from both streets to investigate the monks in the city.
Monks without official registration were all forced to return to lay life and sent back to their native places.
The same rule applied to all circuits, prefectures, and counties.
Monks residing in nearby temples.
Without clear origins, were all arrested and sent to the Jīngzhào Prefecture.
More than 300 newly tonsured monks were beaten to death in the prefecture.
Those who fled and hid.
Dared not walk in the streets.
The troops of the Uighur Kingdom were severely defeated.
The circuit immediately reported to the throne.
Troops from various prefectures and circuits all returned to their respective circuits.
On the third day of the eleventh month.
The 100th-day memorial for Wéixiǎo.
In the twelfth month, I received a letter from Liú Shènyán, the Silla interpreter of Chǔ Prefecture, stating.
Yuánzài Ācārya, who studied at Tiāntái Mountain, said.
He submitted a memorial and sent two disciple monks.
To return to Japan.
His disciples.
Came to Shènyán to seek a ship.
Shènyán.
Arranged for a ship.
Dispatched people to send them off.
They departed this year in the ninth month.
In the second month of the fourth year of Huìchāng, cyclical year Jiǎzǐ.
Pān, the military yāyá of Yuè Prefecture.
While on a mission to deliver medicine.
Brought a letter from Yuánzài Ācārya.
The letter said.
Because clothing and provisions were exhausted.
He sent two disciple monks, Rénhǎo and others.
To their home country.
To request clothing and provisions.
Yāyá Pān said.
The Venerable Zài.
Wished to enter the city to request a document from Yuè Prefecture.
He entrusted it to me.
To present to the Secretariat-Chancellery.
I recently waited for an opportunity.
To enter the Secretariat and submit the document.
The chancellor rejected it.
And did not permit it to be presented to the throne.
Thus, the Venerable’s matter was not accomplished.
In the third month, an imperial decree was issued.
I intend to travel to the Eastern Capital.
And hereby inform all officials that any courtier who dares to remonstrate will be executed and their clan exterminated.
An imperial decree forbade offerings to the Buddha’s tooth relic.
Another decree stated.
Mount Wǔtái in Dài Prefecture.
And Pǔguāngwáng Temple in Sì Prefecture.
Mount Wǔtái in Zhōngnán.
And Fǎmén Temple in Fèngxiáng Prefecture.
Where the Buddha’s finger bone is enshrined.
Are all forbidden from receiving offerings or pilgrimages.
If anyone offers even one coin.
They will receive twenty strokes of the rod on the back.
If any monks or nuns.
Accept even one coin at the aforementioned places.
They will receive twenty strokes of the rod on the back.
All circuits, prefectures, and counties.
If there are people making offerings.
They shall be arrested on the spot.
And receive twenty strokes of the rod on the back.
As a result, these four sacred sites.
Were cut off from visitors.
With no one making offerings, an imperial decree ordered an investigation of the monks at those places.
Those without official verification.
Were to be beaten to death on the spot.
And their names reported to the throne.
For fear that Jiāng Sūn, the rear yāyá of the Lùfǔ Circuit, might be hiding there disguised as a monk.
Chancellors Lǐ Shēn and Lǐ Déyù memorialized to halt the Daoist teachings during the three long months.
Newly established three primal months.
The first month, Shàngyuán.
The sixth month, Zhōngyuán.
The tenth month, Xiàyuán.
The constant practice in the Táng state during the three long months.
Was to forbid killing.
But the current emperor does not follow this.
To suppress the Lùfǔ Circuit, he summoned eighty-one Daoist priests.
And within the palace.
Ordered them to perform a Nine Heavens ritual in an open area.
Eighty beds were stacked high and splendidly arranged.
They performed rituals for twelve hours to worship the Celestial Venerable.
Dried meat, wine, and meat.
Were used to worship the Fire Heaven.
From the first day of the fourth month,
until the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
the Dharma assembly was held.
It was not held inside buildings,
but rituals were performed in open courtyards.
In clear weather, they were scorched by the sun; when it rained, they were drenched.
Among the eighty-one participants, many fell ill.
The current emperor is particularly devoted to Daoism.
He detests Buddhist teachings,
dislikes seeing monks,
and does not wish to hear of the Three Jewels.
In the Chángshēng Hall, where the Dharma assembly was held,
since ancient times,
Buddhist statues and scriptures had been enshrined.
Monks skilled in chanting from various temples along the two main streets were selected,
taking turns to enter,
chanting daily,
ceaselessly day and night.
The current emperor ordered the burning of the scriptures
and the destruction of the Buddhist statues.
The monks were expelled and each returned to their own temple.
In the Dharma assembly hall, statues of the Celestial Worthy and Lǎojūn were installed instead.
Daoist priests were ordered to recite Daoist scriptures
and practice Daoist arts.
According to national custom, every year on the emperor’s birthday,
eminent monks from the two main streets,
along with Daoist priests,
were invited to hold vegetarian feasts and incense ceremonies inside the palace,
with monks expounding the sutras
and debates held between Buddhism and Daoism.
This year, only Daoist priests were invited,
and no monks.
Observing the situation,
from now on,
monks are no longer allowed to enter the palace.
Daoist priests memorialized, saying:
"Confucius said:
The Lǐ clan’s eighteen sons,
when their prosperous fortune is exhausted,
a black-clothed Son of Heaven will govern the country."
"We, your subjects,
humbly consider
that 'black-clothed'
refers to Buddhist monks."
The emperor accepted their words,
and thus grew to despise monks and nuns, thinking:
"The character Lǐ (李) consists of 'eighteen sons'—since I am the eighteenth generation, I fear the Lǐ clan’s fortune may be exhausted.
Could it be that a black-clothed one will seize the throne?"
The Commissioner of Meritorious Works issued notices to all temples,
stating that by imperial decree, monks and nuns were not allowed to be on the streets when the bell tolled.
If they went out,
they must return to their own temples
before the temple bells rang.
They were also not allowed to stay overnight at other temples.
If any monk or nun was found on the streets when the bell tolled,
or stayed overnight at another temple,
they would be punished for violating the decree.
Previously, they were not allowed to leave the temple after noon;
now, they are not allowed to be out when the bell tolls.
In the second month, the emperor visited the Jīnxiān Temple on the right street,
which is a nunnery where there are female Daoist priests.
One was particularly beautiful.
The emperor summoned her and took a liking to her.
He bestowed a thousand bolts of silk upon her,
then ordered the palace officials
to have the temple repaired,
connecting it to the inner palace.
A special Jīnxiān Tower was built.
The temple was originally dilapidated,
but now it was magnificently restored, and the emperor frequently visited.
Later, the emperor visited the Xìngtáng Temple on the left street,
which is a Daoist temple.
He again bestowed a thousand bolts of silk
and ordered special repairs.
A bronze statue of a sage was cast,
made with extraordinary solemnity and beauty, surpassing all the temples in the city.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, offerings were made.
Various temples prepared floral candles,
floral cakes,
artificial flowers, fruits, trees, and the like,
each competing in ingenuity.
It was customary to set up offerings
in front of the Buddha halls.
The entire city would visit the temples to admire them,
making it a grand occasion.
This year, the offerings set up by the temples
surpassed those of previous years.
However, the emperor ordered that all the floral offerings and medicines from the Buddha halls of various temples
be moved to the Xìngtáng Temple
to offer to the Celestial Worthy.
On the fifteenth day, the emperor visited the temple and summoned the people to come and see.
The people cursed, saying:
"They seize Buddhist offerings to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits—who would want to watch?"
The emperor was surprised that the people did not come.
The temples, having had their offerings taken away,
were greatly distressed.
The soldiers of the Dálù Prefecture,
unable to enter enemy territory,
remained at the border.
Frequent imperial decrees urged them, but there was no news.
After conscripting soldiers for a long time,
no news of any punitive expedition was heard.
The frightened soldiers captured herdsmen and farmers at the border
and sent them to the capital,
falsely claiming they had captured rebels.
The emperor bestowed execution swords,
and they were beheaded in the streets, their bodies cut into three pieces.
Soldiers from both armies surrounded and killed them.
Such captives were sent continuously,
and the soldiers never ceased.
Corpses filled the streets,
blood soaking the earth into mud.
Onlookers crowded the roads.
The emperor often came to watch.
Flags and spears crisscrossed in chaotic disarray. It was said
that those sent
were not Táng rebels,
but merely herdsmen and farmers from the border,
wrongly captured.
The state’s soldiers
originally did not enter enemy territory, fearing the emperor would suspect there was no action.
So they falsely captured innocent people
and sent them to the capital.
The brave soldiers of both armies,
whenever they beheaded someone,
would cut out their eyes and flesh to eat.
People in all wards said:
"This year, people in Cháng’ān are eating people."
The emperor summoned the Huáinán military commissioner, Dù Fùmǎ, to the capital.
The chancellor, Lǐ Shēn,
wished to become the Huáinán commissioner.
Following the decree, he escorted Commissioner Dù Fùmǎ to the capital.
Upon his audience, he was appointed chancellor.
He also oversaw the salt and iron monopoly and the state treasury, astonishing all officials.
Since ancient times,
there had never been an instance of a fùmǎ being appointed chancellor.
According to national custom, chancellors were granted the title of Píngzhāng Shì.
Lǐ Déyù memorialized, saying:
"A fùmǎ appointed as chancellor
should not ride in a carriage."
The emperor’s decree was lenient,
but no edict was issued.
Thus, the fùmǎ still could not ride in a carriage.
The soldiers of the Dálù Prefecture
spent two hundred thousand strings of cash daily.
The various prefectures could not transport supplies fast enough.
Moreover, the government warehouses in the capital were nearly depleted.
A decree ordered all government offices to contribute money,
according to the rank of the officials,
to pay varying amounts,
to be used for the soldiers’ provisions.
Officials in all circuits, prefectures, and commanderies
followed the same rule.
Another decree ordered the destruction of all mountain retreats, Lányuě,
common Buddhist halls,
charitable wells,
and village vegetarian halls with fewer than two hundred rooms,
which were not officially registered as temples.
The monks and nuns there were all forced to return to lay life
and assigned to village labor.
Detailed reports were to be submitted.
In Cháng’ān city alone,
there were over three hundred Buddhist halls within the wards, along with scripture towers and the like,
solemnly and properly adorned,
all crafted by renowned artisans.
A single Buddhist hall compound
rivaled major temples in outer prefectures.
By decree, all were to be demolished.
Countless Buddhist halls and compounds throughout the empire
were destroyed.
All victory steles,
monks’ tomb pagodas, and the like
were ordered to be demolished.
The emperor summoned scholars from the Imperial Academy
and those who had passed the imperial examinations,
those with learning,
ordering them to convert to Daoism.
Not a single person entered Daoism.
Since the beginning of this year,
whenever there was little rain,
the Commissioner of Meritorious Works
would issue notices to all temples and Daoist monasteries by imperial decree,
ordering them to chant scriptures to pray for rain.
When rain was successfully invoked,
Daoist priests received special rewards,
while monks and nuns were left idle with nothing.
People in the city whispered:
"When praying for rain, they trouble the monks,
but when giving rewards, they favor the Daoist priests."
In the eighth month, the Empress Dowager passed away.
She was Empress Tàihé of the Guō clan.
Because the Empress Dowager had a mind for the Way,
she believed in the Buddha’s teachings.
Whenever regulations were issued regarding monks and nuns,
she always offered words of remonstrance.
The Emperor ordered poisoned wine to be presented, and she was poisoned to death.
Also, Empress Xiāo of the Yìyáng Hall,
who was the present Emperor’s mother and very beautiful,
the present Emperor summoned and took her as a consort.
But the Empress Dowager did not comply with the order.
The Son of Heaven took a bow and shot her to death.
The arrow pierced her chest, and she died.
Three thousand soldiers from the Tàiyuán Prefecture
had been stationed on guard in the Huíhú territory for three years.
This year, they attacked the Huíhú, defeated them, and returned.
They had not been back at the prefecture for more than a few days,
and had not yet been able to see their relatives,
when the Military Governor dispatched them
to attack Lù Prefecture.
The soldiers repeatedly pleaded, saying:
"We have fought the Huíhú for three years,
enduring hardship and exhaustion.
We have just returned to our hometown,
and have not yet seen our parents and relatives.
We humbly request
that other troops be sent."
The Military Governor refused.
All three thousand men became resentful at once,
and fought their way to the city walls.
The Military Governor reported to the throne,
and they were captured and sent to the capital.
An imperial envoy with troops
met them and interrogated them in detail.
They explained their merits in fighting the Huíhú,
and said it was not right to kill them.
The details were recorded and reported to the throne.
The Emperor did not heed the report.
He bestowed a ceremonial sword
and ordered them to be beheaded and cut into three pieces.
They were executed at the northern street of the Eastern Market, at the execution ground.
Soldiers captured from Lù Prefecture
are often executed at this place.
In the ninth month, Lù Prefecture was heavily defeated.
Those captured included the local Yāyá and generals,
who were sent to the capital
and executed six or seven times.
Later, the head of the rebel leader Liú Cóngjiǎn was brought,
pierced on a three-pronged spearhead,
with a pole over thirty feet high.
His name was inscribed on top,
and it was first paraded around the two markets,
then brought into the palace.
The Son of Heaven sat in the tower of the Yíntái Gate,
and said loudly:
"Zhàoyí has already been defeated.
What remains to be eliminated now
are the Buddhist monasteries throughout the land,
and the regulations regarding monks and nuns are still incomplete.
Do you all know this?"
Several tens of days later,
in accordance with the imperial decree, the wealth, money, treasures, jade pendants, furniture, and other belongings of the Liú family from Lù Prefecture were brought forward.
Each time, seven or eight carts,
decorated with gold and loaded,
were sent into the city
and delivered to the inner treasury.
Qiú Jūnróng’s son, the Regular Attendant who managed affairs within the palace,
drank wine until he was drunk and delirious,
and offended the Emperor’s dignity.
In reply to the Emperor, he said:
"Although the Son of Heaven is so noble,
it was my father who established him on the throne."
The Emperor was enraged
and had him beaten to death on the spot.
He then ordered his wife and daughters to be seized,
banished from the palace,
shaved bald, and made to guard the imperial tombs.
Moreover, the palace eunuchs were ordered to confiscate the family’s property: money, ivory, and jade filled the rooms,
pearls, jade, gold, and silver,
completely filled the storerooms.
The amount of coins, silk, and bolts of cloth was beyond count.
Every day, thirty carts
transported them into the inner treasury.
Within a month,
they could not finish transporting them. As for the remaining treasures, jade pendants,
and rare objects,
they were beyond calculation.
The Emperor went to the inner treasury to look,
clapped his hands in surprise, and said:
"My treasury never had such things before."
All the high-ranking officials lowered their heads and said nothing.
The Daoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn and others memorialized:
"The Buddha was born among the western barbarians.
His teachings speak of non-birth.
But non-birth
is simply death.
He transforms people and makes them enter Nirvana.
Nirvana is death.
He extensively discusses impermanence, suffering, and emptiness,
which is truly demonic and strange.
It does not touch upon the principle of non-action and eternal life.
The Supreme Elderly Lord,
it is heard, was born in China and ascended to the Tàiluó Heaven of Zōngpíng,
free and unfettered, non-acting and spontaneous.
To transform others, he refined immortal elixirs;
taking them leads to eternal life.
He broadly established divine mansions,
bringing boundless benefits.
We request that within the inner palace,
an immortal platform be built,
so that one may refine the body and ascend to the rosy clouds,
free and unfettered in the Nine Heavens.
This would likely bring blessings to the imperial lifespan and ensure the eternal joy of long life."
The Emperor approved the memorial and ordered the two armies to build an immortal platform within the palace.
It was one hundred and fifty feet high.
Construction began in the tenth month.
Every day, three thousand soldiers from the Left and Right Shéncè Armies were used to carry earth and build it.
The Emperor was eager for it to be completed early,
and every day there was an imperial decree urging construction.
The Dū Yúhóu of the two armies
held rods to supervise the work.
The Emperor, while passing by, saw this
and asked a senior palace official:
"Who are those holding rods?"
The senior official memorialized:
"They are the Dū Yúhóu of the Imperial Guard,
managing the platform construction."
The Emperor declared:
"I do not want you managing with rods.
You must carry earth yourselves."
So they were made to carry earth.
Later, the Emperor again visited the construction site.
The Emperor himself took a bow and, for no reason, shot and killed one Yúhóu.
Such extreme lack of virtue!
Since last year,
lectures in the two streets have ceased entirely.
Since ascending the throne,
he has been fond of making excursions.
Apart from the four seasons and eight festivals, he goes out every one or two days.
Each time he travels, he orders the various monasteries
to prepare beds and mats,
felt carpets,
decorated curtains and pavilions,
and set out bowls, plates, tables, chairs, and the like.
For each excursion,
each monastery spends four to five hundred strings of cash,
and it is never enough.
An imperial decree ordered their destruction.
Buddhist scriptures and statues from small monasteries throughout the land were moved to large monasteries.
Bells were sent to Daoist temples.
Monks and nuns from the destroyed monasteries who behaved crudely and did not follow the precepts,
regardless of age,
were all forced to return to lay life,
sent back to their native places,
and enrolled in local corvée labor.
Those who were old and had observed the precepts
were assigned to large monasteries.
Even if they observed the precepts,
if they were young,
they were all forced to return to lay life,
and sent back to their native places.
In the city, thirty-three small monasteries were destroyed.
The regulations regarding monks and nuns
were all in accordance with the imperial decree.
In the eleventh month, an imperial decree was issued:
"Because Zhàoyí
and the bandits have been defeated,
I will hold the southern suburban sacrifice
in the first month of next year.
I order all officials
to inform their respective offices
to make early preparations."
All departments, in accordance with the decree,
repaired bridges, roads, and streets,
so that people, horses, carriages, and oxen could not pass.
The southern suburban altar
was specially repaired and built.
On all four sides of the altar, decorated curtains were hung.
Pavilions, towers, and city encampments
all followed the style of the inner palace.
All departments were extremely busy.
In the fifth year of the Huìchāng era, the cyclical year being yǐchǒu, on the third day of the first month.
The southern suburb worship ceremony was held.
The ceremonial guards and majestic rituals.
Were entirely the same as in the first year.
Monks and nuns were not permitted to watch.
Moreover, there were existing regulations.
Prohibiting monks and nuns from leaving the temples after noon.
And also forbidding them to violate the fasting bell.
Or to stay overnight at other temples.
Therefore, monks were unable to watch the southern suburb ceremony.
The construction of the Immortal Terrace was nearing completion.
An imperial decree ordered Daoist priests to refine the elixir of immortality.
The chief Daoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn memorialized, saying:
"There is a certain type of immortal medicine.
That is completely unavailable in this country.
Only in the Tǔfān country.
Does this medicine exist.
I request to personally go to Tǔfān.
To gather this medicine."
The two army eunuch commanders refused.
And instead memorialized, saying:
"Sending someone else would be acceptable.
However, Zhào Guīzhēn, as the leader in seeking immortality,
Should not go personally."
The emperor decreed in accordance with the eunuch commanders' memorial.
And did not allow him to go.
There was an imperial inquiry:
"What medicines are used in seeking immortality?
Provide a detailed list and submit a memorial."
The Daoist priests submitted the names of the medicines:
Ten catties of plum seed coats,
Ten catties of peach fuzz,
Ten catties of raw chicken membrane,
Ten catties of turtle hair,
Ten catties of rabbit horns, and so on.
An imperial order was issued to search for them in the medicinal markets.
All claimed they did not exist.
Because of this, official reports were beaten,
Causing endless vexation.
Thus, they searched everywhere.
But still could not obtain them.
From before the Cold Food Festival,
It had been customary to grant seven days of leave according to regulations.
The three thousand laborers building the terrace, being government troops, were not granted release during the Cold Food Festival.
Resentful, they grasped their tools and prostrated themselves.
The three thousand men simultaneously cried out in unison.
The emperor was frightened.
He bestowed three bolts of silk to each man.
And granted three days of leave.
The third day of the third month.
The construction of the platform was completed.
It was named the Ascension to Immortality Platform.
The sovereign ascended the platform.
The two army commanders-in-chief,
the various high-ranking officials,
and the Daoist priests,
followed the emperor up.
The two army commanders-in-chief said to Zhào Guīzhēn,
"Today the Ascension to Immortality Platform is completed.
We wonder if you gentlemen will succeed in seeking immortality."
Guīzhēn lowered his head and did not speak.
It is said
that the Ascension to Immortality Platform was one hundred and fifty chǐ high.
Its top was circular,
level with the foundation of a seven-bay hall.
Upon it, a five-peak tower was built.
People both inside and outside
could all see from afar the solitary mountain towering high.
They transported massive stones from Zhōngnán Shān
to form four mountain cliffs.
Niche caves and winding paths
were carved and decorated with exquisite craftsmanship.
They then planted pines, cypresses, and other rare and extraordinary trees.
It was laughably satisfying.
Thereupon an edict was issued:
Ordering seven Daoist priests
to perform alchemical practices and seek immortality upon the platform.
Another edict was issued to all the monasteries and temples in the land:
They were not permitted to maintain estates or manors.
Furthermore, an order was given to investigate and audit all the monasteries and temples in the land,
including the number of slaves and servants, as well as money, goods, grain, bolts of silk, and other items.
Each item was to be verified truthfully and recorded in detail,
and reported for the emperor to hear.
The monasteries and temples within the capital city
were entrusted to the two army commanders-in-chief for investigation and audit.
The monasteries and temples in the various prefectures and districts were delegated to the Secretariat-Chancellery for investigation and audit.
Moreover, regarding the slaves and servants of the monasteries and temples in the capital city, they were divided into three categories:
Those with skills or crafts were to be conscripted into the army.
Those without skills who were young and strong were to be sold.
The old and weak were to become palace slaves.
There was lamentation, fathers separated from sons.
Such is the present time.
The Commissioner of Merits and Virtues issued notices to the various temples:
Slaves and servants were to form groups of five as mutual guarantors.
If one person from a guarantor group went missing,
a fine of two thousand strings of cash was to be imposed.
The funds and goods of the various temples,
along with the money from selling slaves and servants,
were all to be confiscated by the government.
They were intended to be used for the salaries and allowances of the hundred officials.
Another edict ordered all the monasteries and temples in the land:
Monks and nuns under forty years of age
were all to be compelled to return to lay life.
They were to be sent back to their native places in succession.
The sovereign again ascended the Ascension to Immortality Platform.
He ordered the musicians
to push the Left Army Commander-in-Chief off.
The musicians were unwilling to push him.
The emperor asked, "I command you to push.
Why do you not obey?"
The musicians memorialized, saying:
"The Commander-in-Chief is an important minister of the state.
We dare not push him down."
The Son of Heaven, angry, had them beaten twenty strokes on the back.
On the platform, he reproached the Daoist priests, saying:
"I have ascended this platform twice.
Why is it that not one of you gentlemen has ascended to immortality?"
The Daoist priests memorialized, saying:
"It is because the Buddhist teaching in the country
runs parallel with the Daoist teaching.
The heterodox influence is too strong,
hindering the path to immortality.
Therefore, ascension to immortality cannot be achieved."
The sovereign announced to the Commissioners of Merits and Virtues of the two streets:
"Do you know?
If I were Hé Shī, I would want none of them."
Several days later, an edict was issued:
All monks and nuns in the land,
those fifty years of age and below,
were all to be compelled to return to lay life.
They were to be sent back to their native places in succession, and this was completed.
Afterwards, there was an edict stating:
All monks and nuns in the land,
those fifty years of age and above,
who do not possess a certificate from the Bureau of Sacrifices,
are all to be compelled to return to lay life.
They are to be sent back to their native places in succession.
Those who possess a certificate from the Bureau of Sacrifices
are to be delegated to their respective prefectures and counties for detailed verification.
If discrepancies are found,
they are all to be compelled to return to lay life.
They are to be sent back to their native places in succession.
Monks and nuns within the capital city
are delegated to the Commissioner of Merits and Virtues
to handle according to this regulation by verifying and listing them.
The Secretariat-Chancellery, in accordance with the edict, issued notices to the various circuits, and this was completed.
Regarding the monks and nuns in the city,
the Commissioner of Merits and Virtues verified and listed them
with extreme strictness.
Moreover, he determined the number of monks and nuns without certificates from the Bureau of Sacrifices,
recorded them in detail, and submitted a memorial.
He then issued notices to the various temples:
They were to move their furniture and belongings.
Those who possessed certificates from the Bureau of Sacrifices
were all to be summoned into the army headquarters for detailed verification.
If on the certificate from the Bureau of Sacrifices there was the slightest stain or smudge, or if the birth year differed from that in the merit records and guarantor documents,
and discrepancies were found,
they were all included in the number to return to lay life.
If no discrepancies were found,
they were then entered into the army records and not released.
Consequently, the monks and nuns of the various temples were all without their certificates of ordination.
Everyone said:
"Not returning the certificates of ordination
is a scheme to not retain monks and nuns.
Confiscating the slaves, money, and goods of the temples
is an omen of destroying the temple buildings."
The emperor announced:
"The pit for moving earth is extremely deep,
causing people fear and unease.
I wish to have it filled.
On the day of the platform sacrifice,
under the pretext of holding a vegetarian feast to celebrate the platform,
summon all the monks and nuns of the two streets to gather in the Left Army headquarters, behead them, and use them to fill the pit."
Jiǎn Shūbǔ secretly memorialized, saying:

On October 6th,

The lecturer of Kannonji
