Ennin,
known in Japan as Jikaku Daishi,
was a famous monk of the Tendai sect.
He came to China to study during the reign of Emperor Wenzong of Táng,
staying for ten years,
and returned to Japan in the early Dàzhōng era of Emperor Xuānzong.
He authored the four-volume "Record of a Pilgrimage to Táng in Search of the Law,"
an important historical source on the Táng dynasty recorded by a foreigner.
Here, we briefly examine his life,
and discuss and quote from his travel diary in Táng as this piece.
The monk Yuánrén, whose surname was Wángshēng,

was born in 794 CE (the thirteenth year of the Enryaku era of Emperor Kammu of Japan, corresponding to the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong of the Tang Dynasty) in Tsuga District, Shimotsuke Province.
He lost his father in his childhood,
was intelligent and quick-witted by nature,
and had a gentle and refined demeanor.
At the age of nine, his elder brother taught him the classics and histories.
In the same district, at Daicí Temple, there was a monk named Guǎngzhì,
who was a third-generation disciple of the Tang Dynasty monk Jiànzhēn.
His virtue and learning were comprehensive and profound.
He raised Yuánrén as his dharma heir,
and thus Yuánrén devoted himself exclusively to the study of Buddhist scriptures.
At the age of fifteen,
he ascended Mount Hiei in the capital and paid homage to the Great Master Chuándēng, Zuìchéng,
who instructed him in the profound wisdom of the śamatha-vipaśyanā meditation and great samādhi.
He distinguished himself, rising above his peers.
When people came seeking instruction on śamatha-vipaśyanā,
Master Chuándēng would often have Rén (Yuánrén) lecture on it,
while he himself sat nearby listening and verifying,
and this became the regular practice.
In the fourth year of the Kōnin era,
at the age of twenty,
he passed the official examination.
In the first month of the following year,
he received ordination and upheld the śrāmaṇera precepts.
In the seventh year, he received the full precepts (bhikṣu ordination) at Tōdai-ji.
After Zuìchéng's parinirvāṇa,
he studied and practiced even more diligently,
and established lecture platforms in various places.
In the third year of the Jōwa era of Emperor Ninmyō, he received an imperial edict to travel to Tang China to seek further instruction.
In the sixth month of the fifth year,
he accompanied Fujiwara no Tsunetsugu, the head of Japan's eighteenth embassy to Tang China, on the westward voyage.
He was forty-five years old at the time.
After traveling in Tang for ten years, he returned to Japan,
where he greatly propagated the Buddhist Dharma.
He received favor and treatment from Emperors Montoku and Seiwa,
was honored as the Great Master Chuándēng,
was appointed head of the Tendai school,
petitioned for the establishment of the Sōji-in temple,
performed offerings for the emperor,
and taught his disciples samādhi.
He built the Jōgyō-dō hall,
and greatly organized the regulations for exoteric and esoteric teachings.
He constructed the Monju-rō tower,
laying its foundation with soil and stones he brought back from Mount Wǔtái.
The Japanese Tendai school was founded by Zuìchéng,
but it was Yuánrén who truly brought it to prosperity and great completion.
On the fourteenth day of the first month in the sixth year of the Jōgan era of Emperor Seiwa,
he passed into stillness at Enryaku-ji in the capital,
at the age of seventy-one.
One day before his passing, he conferred the secret seal and abhiṣeka upon his eminent disciple Jōsai.
Yuánrén's bearing was gentle and serene,
yet inwardly firm and resolute.
His writings were extremely numerous.
According to the "Chronological Table of Japanese Literary Figures" compiled by Akahori,
his commentaries, subcommentaries, and personal records totaled ninety-four works,
in one hundred and fifty-three volumes.
The "Commentaries on the Vajraśekhara and Susiddhikara Sūtras" in seven volumes,
and the "Treatise Elucidating the Mahāyāna Precepts" in eight volumes
were all published by imperial command.
His "Record of a Pilgrimage to Tang China in Search of the Dharma" is also renowned.
Critics praised him, saying: "He crossed the vast ocean in person,
trod upon sacred caves with his feet,
approached those of superior wisdom to partake of their teachings,
inquired of great scholars to exhaust the sources.
The profound Dharma of the Three Mysteries,
he transmitted authentically, distinguishing them clearly.
The perfectly penetrating teaching of the One Vehicle,
he revived to its utmost depths, leaving nothing out."
In the seventh month of the eighth year, an imperial edict ordered the offering of one thousand copies of the Lotus Sūtra at Sōji-in.
A posthumous title was conferred, stating: "The late Tendai head, Yuánrén: his compassionate heart was unfathomable,
his wings of wisdom soared high.
Reaching Mount Wǔtái to seek guidance,
his sincerity was akin to piercing one's neck;
expounding the Three Mysteries to propagate the teaching,
his work was to enhance its splendor.
He turned the great Brahma-wheel,
roared the true lion's roar.
We, in our humble person, frequently received his compassionate gaze in the past.
Regretting the sudden separation from his protection,
how can our thoughts of honoring and adorning him ever be exhausted?
He should be posthumously awarded the title Dharma Seal Great Monk,
and further granted the posthumous name Great Master Cíjué."
The details are recorded in works such as the "Biography of Great Master Cíjué,"
"Volume Three of the Origins of the Transmission of Buddhism in the Three Countries,"
"Volume Three of the Genkō Shakusho,"
"Volume Six of the Biographies of Eminent Japanese Monks,"
and "Huá Fāng Yú Huī."
In the first year of Emperor Ninmyō of Japan,
Councilor Fujiwara no Tsunetsugu was appointed as ambassador to Tang.
On the second day of the seventh month of the following year, four ships set sail together,
with Yuánrén among the party.
They encountered danger and ship damage,
and all turned back.
In the seventh month of the fourth year, they set sail again,
but encountered adverse winds and did not succeed.
Finally, on the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the fifth year,
they again boarded the first and fourth ships departing from Hakata in Kyushu,
marking the third attempt to begin the journey.
Yuánrén's "Record of a Pilgrimage to Tang" begins from this day.
On the twenty-second day of the sixth month, they set sail on the open sea.
The winds and waves were extremely fierce,
and they fully experienced hardships and dangers.
On the second day of the seventh month in the third year of the Kaicheng era of Emperor Wenzong of Tang,
they arrived at Hailing County, Yangzhou Prefecture, Huainan Circuit.
The ambassador, through a memorial by Li Deyu, Military Governor of Huainan, obtained permission to proceed to Chang'an.
Yuánrén requested permission to make a pilgrimage to Mount Tiāntāi,
and remained in Yangzhou awaiting imperial approval.
During this time, he studied Siddhaṃ script with Sōei,
and obtained the two maṇḍalas of the Garbhadhātu and Vajradhātu,
designs for various deity altars,
portraits of eminent monks, and twenty-one kinds of relics,
along with one hundred and twenty-eight texts including sūtras, treatises, commentaries, and subcommentaries,
totaling one hundred and ninety-eight volumes.
Later, he met the ambassador in Chuzhou,
but his request to pilgrimage to Mount Tiāntāi
was ultimately not granted.
Disappointed, he boarded the embassy ship for the return journey.
When the ship anchored at Donghai County, Haizhou,
Yuánrén, along with his disciples Isei and Gyō, and the sailor Tei Yūman, used a pretext to secretly disembark and go ashore.
They were discovered by the Haizhou authorities
and inspected by the prefect.
It happened that the second ship of the Japanese embassy arrived off the coast of Haizhou,
so they were escorted back onto the ship.
On the eighteenth day of the fourth month, they reached the coast of Muping County, Dengzhou.
The narrative of the first volume of the pilgrimage record ends here.
On the seventh day of the sixth month in the fourth year of Kaicheng,
the ship anchored at Chishan Bay in Wendeng County, Dengzhou.
At Chishan, there was a Lotus Sūtra Temple built by the Silla man Jang Bogo,
with over thirty monks in residence,
seven of whom were Japanese.
Hearing this, Yuánrén was moved.
He again bid farewell to the ambassador,
disembarked and went to the Lotus Sūtra Temple,
where he stayed for over a year.
He petitioned Zhang Yong, the Military Commissioner of Pinglu Circuit concurrently in charge of military affairs in Dengzhou and a yāyá official.
Zhang Yong had previously been an envoy to Japan
and admired Yuánrén's fervent sincerity.
He assisted him,
and thus Yuánrén obtained permission to pilgrimage to Mount Wǔtái.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of Kaicheng, he traveled north from Dengzhou,
passing through Qingzhou,
Zizhou,
Qizhou,
Dezhou,
Beizhou,
Jizhou,
and Xingtang in Zhaozhou,
heading northwest towards the Taihang Mountains.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month, he reached the foothills of Mount Qīngliáng.
The pilgrimage record states: "In the valleys and ravines of the mountains,
the trees stand tall and straight;
there is not a single crooked or bent tree.
Upon entering the realm of the great sage,
even upon seeing the lowliest of people,
one dares not harbor a contemptuous heart.
If one encounters a donkey or other beast,
one also gives rise to a questioning mind,
fearing it might be a manifestation of Mañjuśrī.
Everything seen with raised eyes
gives rise to the thought that it is a transformation of Mañjuśrī.
This sacred and numinous land
causes people to naturally give rise to a heart of reverence and esteem."
He thus expressed his utmost sincerity.
The second volume of the diary ends here.
On the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month, Ennin gazed upon Central Terrace,
prostrated himself on the ground and paid respects from afar,
tears flowing unbidden.
He then trekked to the Northwest, East, and other terraces,
touring the sacred sites.
He visited renowned masters such as Xuánjiàn and
Zhìyuǎn,
presenting thirty points of doubt from Enryaku-ji for explanation.
He copied secret texts of the Tiāntāi school,
obtaining thirty-four works in thirty-seven volumes.
He stayed in the mountains for over fifty days.
On the first day of the seventh month,
he collected spirit stones and soil from the lion's footprint as mementos.
Bidding farewell to the sacred mountain,
he headed west toward Cháng'ān.
Passing through Xīnzhōu,
Tàiyuán,
Hézhōng Fǔ,
he crossed the Yellow River at Lóngmén.
Traversing Cháoyì,
Yuèzhōu,
he finally arrived at the long-dreamed-of capital of the Great Táng on the twenty-third day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Kāichéng era.
He petitioned Qiú Shìliáng, the Commissioner of Merit for the Left Street,
and was assigned to reside at Zīshèng Temple.
At that time, Cháng'ān was filled with renowned monks,
competing in brilliance like a forest of steeds.
Ennin studied the two secret teachings from Venerable Yuánzhèng at the Translation Hall of Dàxīngshàn Temple and
Venerable Yìzhēn at the East Pagoda Hall of Qīnglóng Temple,
inquired about the Vajra precepts from Fǎrùn at Qīnglóng Temple,
received the Womb Realm rituals from Fǎquán at Xuánfǎ Temple,
and learned the practice of cessation and contemplation from Zōngyǐng at Lǐquán Temple.
Wénwù Ācārya of Dàxīngshàn Temple and
Yuánjiǎn Ācārya of Dà'ānguó Temple,
both provided him with enlightenment.
He also restudied Siddhaṃ under the Tripiṭaka master Bǎoyuè from Southern India,
receiving correct pronunciation orally.
He obtained the two maṇḍalas of the Womb and Vajra realms,
altar diagrams of various deities,
ritual implements, and twenty-one other items,
and collected 423 texts of sūtras, treatises, commentaries, and biographies,
totaling 559 volumes.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Huìchāng era under Emperor Wǔzōng,
Ennin had been in Táng for three years,
having thoroughly mastered the principles of the Three Vehicles,
and suddenly attained the gate of non-duality.
His wisdom surpassed others,
and his learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular studies.
He then petitioned the Commissioner of Merit to request permission to return to his country,
but it was not granted.
Since Emperor Wǔzōng assumed power,
actions to suppress Buddhism and persecute monks
grew increasingly severe day by day.
On the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month in the third year of Huìchāng,
a decree was issued to thoroughly investigate foreign monks in all temples.
Ennin submitted a statement explaining his situation.
The records of the third volume of the pilgrimage diary end here.
On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month in the third year of Huìchāng,
his disciple Wéixiǎo passed away,
having suffered from a chronic illness for seven months.
Ennin arranged the funeral,
feeling increasingly sorrowful and resolved to hasten his return.
Emperor Wǔzōng's destruction of temples and expulsion of monks
reached its peak in the fifth year of Huìchāng.
Ennin was also ordered to return to lay life at this time,
which provided an opportunity for him to return to his country.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, he departed from Cháng'ān.
Devotees such as Yáng Jìngzhī and
Lǐ Yuánzuǒ bid him farewell,
parting with deep reluctance, saying:
"The teachings of our country
will follow the Venerable Master eastward!"
Yuánzuǒ requested his monastic robe,
placing it on his head to console his parting sorrow.
Ennin grew his hair and changed into lay clothing,
passing through Zhèngzhōu,
Biànzhōu,
Sìzhōu, and then down to Wéiyáng.
He then exited Chǔzhōu,
Hǎizhōu,
traversed Mìzhōu,
Láizhōu, and arrived at the Silla Affairs Office in Wéndēng County,
waiting for a convenient ship.
Although he received protection from Military Governor Zhāng Yǒng,
he endured repeated hardships,
and ultimately had no opportunity to sail back.
Three years passed slowly,
until the ninth month of the first year of the Dàzhōng era under Emperor Xuānzōng,
when he finally boarded a ship bound for Japan with Silla people and returned east.
He shaved his head and changed back into black robes,
departing from Chìshān Port,
and arrived at Hakata in Chikuzen on the seventeenth day of the ninth month,
which was the fourteenth year of the Jōwa era in Japan.
The Grand Council of State ordered Dazaifu to welcome Ennin to the capital.
Ennin then offered silk and cloth to the great deities of Taisan-ji, Sumiyoshi, and Kashii,
giving thanks for divine protection.
The pilgrimage diary concludes on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month of that year.
The drafting began on the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of Jōwa,
and by this point, it had spanned nine years and seven months.
The places he traveled to in Táng,
according to modern administrative divisions,
involved seven provinces: Jiāngsū,
Shāndōng,
Héběi,
Shānxī,
Shǎnxī,
Hénán,
and Ānhuī.
The four-volume "Record of a Pilgrimage to Táng"
is Ennin's diary of his travels in Táng,
covering two countries,
spanning ten years in time.
Although not without interruptions,
the arrangement by year and month
is orderly and clear.
This work has only gained widespread recognition in recent years.
The manuscript in Ennin's own hand was originally kept at Enryaku-ji in Kyōto,
but it is no longer extant.
The "Biography of Master Jìjué"
was written forty-nine years after the master's passing,
clearly recording the events of his journey to Táng,
entirely based on this diary.
During the Northern Sòng dynasty, the Ācārya Chéngxún, who traveled to Sòng,
was ordered by Emperor Shénzōng
to present the first three volumes of this work in the fifth year of the Xīníng era,
as seen in his "Record of Pilgrimages to Tiāntāi and Wǔtái Shān"
volume four.
Thus, this work had long been stored in the Sòng imperial library.
The authors of Nichiren Shōnin's "Risshō Ankoku Ron,"
"Eigaku Ki,"
and "Genkō Shakusho Shōko"
all cited this work,
proving its long circulation.
There are two extant ancient manuscripts today:
one is the Kyōto Tō-ji Kanchi-in version,
and the other is the version held by the Ikeda-Nagata family.
The Tō-ji Kanchi-in version was copied by the Dharma Seal Kén'in in the fourth year of the Shōō era in Japan.
The fourth volume has a colophon stating:
"Copied on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of Shōō at the Chōraku-ji quarters, wiping old eyes to complete the writing.
Followed the original copy,
later generations may collate with the verified version."
Dharma Seal, Great Venerable, Henjō Kongō Kén'in recorded this.
At the end of the second and third volumes, it is written:
"Collated once with a manuscript,
Kén'in."
The fourth volume also has a small-character colophon:
"Collated with a manuscript,
only noting uncertain matters."
A note on the left side states:
"This is the version of the Second-Rank Prelate Kaku Kan."
There is no information available about Dharma Master Kén'in.
Chōraku-ji is in Maruyama, Kyōto,
originally a Tiāntāi school temple,
and Kén'in was likely its abbot.
He used Prelate Kaku Kan's version for collation and reference,
but the original source is unknown.
The "Eigaku Yōki"
records that Dharma Seal Kaku Kan restored the Great Lecture Hall,
the Mañjuśrī Hall,
the Sōji-in,
and the Mañjuśrī lion statues, which were burned down in the second year of the Genkyū era.
The Prelate Kaku Kan mentioned in Dharma Seal Kén'in's colophon
is likely the same Dharma Seal Kaku Kan who transmitted the copy.
The fourth year of Shōō, when Dharma Seal Kén'in copied the text, was over 430 years after Ennin's passing.
This so-called Kamakura-period ancient manuscript
is designated as a national treasure by the Japanese.
In December of the fifteenth year of the Taishō era, the Tōyō Bunko in Tokyo published a facsimile edition of 300 copies,
accompanied by a one-volume explanatory text written by Dr. Okada Masayuki, professor at Tokyo Imperial University,
making a total of five volumes.
The Ikeda-Nagata family version has a colophon by Prelate Chōkai from the second year of the Bunka era, stating:
"Copied on the thirteenth day of the second month in the second year of Bunka, using the version from Matsuzen-in in Iimidani, Mount Hiei.
Dharma Seal Prelate Chōkai, resident of Hiekin Tsukane-ji."
Tsukane-ji is a Tiāntāi school temple in Kita Saku District, Shinano Province.
Thus, the Ikeda version was copied by Prelate Chōkai borrowing the Matsuzen-in version.
However, the Matsuzen-in version on Mount Hiei is now lost.
Although the Ikeda version is later in time,
it has fewer errors and omissions compared to the Tō-ji Kanchi-in version.
The Matsuzen version it was based on
may have been an ancient copy,
and thus deserves attention in research.
Although the Tōji Kanchi-in manuscript is an ancient transcription,
the copy it was based on
seems to contain many errors and omissions.
Even after collating it with the Kan'en Sōjō version,
numerous errors and omissions remain.
Furthermore, due to being transcribed in old age,
the handwriting is blurred,
making it difficult to read.
It is likely that Ennin's original manuscript
already contained unavoidable errors and omissions.
The text now contains an extremely large number of phonetic loan characters,
such as "Nánzhào"
written as "Nánzhào" (南照),
"Lù Fǔ"
abbreviated as "Lù Fǔ" (路府),
"Liú Cóngjiàn"
written as "Liú Cóngjiǎn" (劉從簡),
and so on.
The "Record of Ascending Mount Wǔtái" from the 28th day of the fourth month to the 16th day of the fifth month in the fifth year of the Kāichéng era
is duplicated at the end of the second volume and the beginning of the third volume,
with the texts differing in detail and brevity.
This was likely due to deletions in the original draft,
rather than copyists transmitting variant texts.
Due to repeated copying and transmission,
disordered bamboo slips reappearing
is a frequent occurrence.
For example, the petition for a travel pass submitted by Ennin to the military governor of Dēngzhōu on the 5th day of the third month in the fifth year of the Kāichéng era in the second volume
reappears under the entry for the 17th day of the second month of the same year.
The record for the 14th day of the third month in the fifth year of the Kāichéng era in the second volume
has the first half mixed with the record for the 16th day,
followed by the reappearance of the records for the 29th day of the second month,
the 1st day of the third month,
and the 2nd day of the third month.
This is then followed by the latter half of the record for the 14th day of the third month and the events of the 15th
and 16th days,
making it the most severe case of disordered slips.
The Ikeda Nagata version has fewer erroneous characters.
Judging from the fact that the petition to the military governor of Dēngzhōu on the 5th day of the third month in the fifth year of the Kāichéng era in the second volume does not reappear,
the Shōzen-in version, the Kan'en version, and the Tōji Kanchi-in version
seem to derive from two different sources.
However, they share some instances of disordered slips,
likely due to oversights by the original transcriber of the draft.
The Pilgrimage Record was not published until recent years.
First, it was included in the Zoku Gunsho Ruijū by the Kokusho Kankōkai.
Later, the Documents Section of the Tendai Sect Administration appended the Ikeda version to the Shiming Yuxia.
Takakusu Junjirō compiled the Dai Nihon Bukkyō Zensho,
including it as the first volume in the Yuhōden Sōsho series,
using the Tōji Kanchi-in version as the base text,
and collating it with the Ikeda version published in Shiming Yuxia and the Kokusho Kankōkai edition.
Those who participated in the collation included Tsuji Zennosuke, Wada Hidematsu,
Kuroita Katsumi,
and Fujita Yasu, among others.
All were erudite scholars.
There is a postscript by Takakusu Junjirō dated June 30, 1915.
Okada Masayuki once began writing annotations and explanations,
but passed away before completing the book.
The Pilgrimage Record spans a long period
and covers a wide range of topics.
From the interactions between the two countries
to the customs, rituals,
governmental systems,
local organizations,
political measures,
religious issues,
diplomacy, and international wars of the Great Táng,
it largely records firsthand observations and accounts,
jotted down as notes.
Correspondence and official documents exchanged
are also often transcribed in full,
aiding in the study of the formats of public and private documents of the time.
Although some of the recorded facts may be based on erroneous rumors or hearsay,
there is much that can supplement historical records.
In ancient Japan, the number of diplomats,
studying monks,
and students
who traveled to China was considerable,
but few left behind important records. These include Master Zhìchéng's "Xínglì Chāo" from the Táng dynasty,
the Acharya Jōjin's "San Tendai Godaisan Ki" from the Sòng dynasty,
Monk Ruìxīn's "Rù Táng Jì" from the Míng dynasty,
and Monk Sakugen's "Shodoshū"
and "Saidoshū,"
along with Ennin's work,
collectively known as the Five Great Travelogues.
In terms of scale
and the abundance of historical traces,
Ennin's work truly stands out as the finest.
The facts he records
often provide material for historical research,
supplementing deficiencies in Chinese records.
For example, the entry for the fourth month of the fifth year of the Huìchāng era in the fourth volume states:
"The Left and Right Shéncè Armies
are the emperor's guard armies.
Each army has one hundred thousand troops.
Since ancient times, rulers have often faced rebellions from ministers,
so since these armies were established,
no one has dared to seize the throne.
An imperial edict bestowed seals. Whenever a new Zhōngwèi (commander) assumed office,
according to the edict, troops and horses were dispatched to welcome the seal.
They handled separate official matters
and were not subordinate to the Nán Sī (Southern Administration).
At the beginning of the fourth month this year (the fifth year of Huìchāng),
an edict demanded the seals of the two armies.
The Zhōngwèi refused to surrender the seals.
The edict repeatedly demanded them.
The intention of the edict was to take the guard army seals and entrust them to the Zhōngshū Ménxià (Secretariat-Chancellery) for management,
so that all military affairs
would be handled according to the decisions of the chief ministers.
The Zhōngwèi of the Left Army agreed to surrender the seal,
but the Zhōngwèi of the Right Army refused.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
'On the day the seal was welcomed,
troops and horses were dispatched to welcome it.
On the day the seal is surrendered,
troops and horses must also be mobilized to surrender it.'
The Zhōngwèi intended that if the edict granted permission,
he would use this as a pretext to mobilize troops and stir up trouble.
He then ordered his subordinates
to secretly arrange troops and horses.
The sovereign, fearing this, temporarily ceased demanding the seal."
This describes the covert struggle between Emperor Wǔzōng and the eunuch-led Shéncè Army.
Wǔzōng wanted to reclaim the official seals
and entrust military authority to the chief ministers,
but the Right Army Zhōngwèi, Yú Hóngzhì, secretly plotted to defy the order,
and the matter was thus thwarted.
Even with Wǔzōng's bravery and prowess,
there were things he could do nothing about.
This occurred two years after Qiú Shìliáng's death,
a time when eunuch power was waning.
The New Táng History biography of Qiú Shìliáng records:
"Wǔzōng was clear-sighted and decisive.
Although he owed his accession to Shìliáng's support,
he inwardly disliked him,
outwardly showing him honor and favor."
This was likely unavoidable.
The Huìchāng anti-Buddhist movement
resulted in the demolition of over 4,600 temples nationwide,
the return to lay life of 260,500 monks and nuns,
who were registered as tax-paying households,
the destruction of over 40,000 private monasteries and hermitages,
the confiscation of tens of millions of qǐng of fertile land,
and the conversion of 150,000 slaves into tax-paying households.
Manichaeism, Nestorianism, Zoroastrianism, and other religions
were also implicated and eradicated.
This was truly a major event in religious history,
yet very few Táng dynasty works record it.
This is because Wǔzōng implemented the thorough eradication of Buddhism in the fifth year of Huìchāng,
but died suddenly in the third month of the sixth year after taking Daoist elixirs.
Emperor Xuānzōng succeeded to the throne,
immediately executed the Daoist priest Liú Xuánjìng and others,
and restored Buddhist temples.
From then on, both court and commoners avoided speaking of these events.
The Old Táng History
and the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government
both record the main points under the fifth year of Huìchāng.
However, the events actually began at the start of Wǔzōng's reign.
The Pilgrimage Record provides particularly detailed accounts.
Here, the relevant events are compiled as follows:
On the 11th day of the sixth month of the first year of Huìchāng, the current emperor's birthday,
a vegetarian feast was held within the palace.
Great Virtuous Ones from both streets and Daoist priests gathered to discuss scriptures,
engaging in four pairs of debates.
Two Daoist priests were bestowed purple robes,
but Buddhist Great Virtuous Ones were not allowed to wear them at all.
The Tripiṭaka master from Southern India, Bǎoyuè, entered the palace to face the sovereign.
He took out a memorial from his bosom and presented it, requesting to return to his homeland.
He had not first consulted the Kāifǔ (a high official).
Angered,
on the fifth day, he was imprisoned in the army for the crime of bypassing officials.
Consequently, three of Bǎoyuè's disciples were each sentenced to seven strokes of the rod,
the interpreter monk received ten strokes,
the Tripiṭaka master was not beaten,
but was not allowed to return to his country.
On the third day of the third month,
Chief Minister Lǐ submitted a memorial regarding regulations on monks and nuns.
An edict was issued to send away those without proper registration,
and unnamed monks were not permitted to keep acolytes or novices.
On the ninth day of the tenth month, an imperial edict was issued:
all Buddhist monks and nuns in the realm who practice alchemy, incantations, breath-control techniques, evade military service,
bear scars from caning,
have tattoos, engage in miscellaneous crafts,
have previously committed adultery or kept wives,
or do not uphold the precepts,
are all to be secularized by edict.
If monks or nuns possess money, goods, grain, land, or estates,
these shall be confiscated by the state.
If they cling to their wealth
and willingly return to secular life,
they may also be allowed to be secularized by edict,
and registered for the twice-a-year tax and corvée labor.
The edict text is recorded separately.
The Commissioners of Merit for the two wards of the capital city posted notices to all monasteries,
forbidding the release of monks and nuns,
and keeping the monastery gates closed.
The monk Xuànxuán petitioned, claiming he could make a sword-wheel
and lead troops to attack the Uyghur Khaganate.
An edict ordered that monk to attempt making the sword-wheel,
but he failed.
Furthermore, upon hearing the report of Chancellor Lǐ Shēn,
this regulation was initiated.
That monk Xuànxuán had deceived and embezzled the property of monks and nuns.
In accordance with the edict's regulations for the realm,
a communique was issued by the Secretariat-Chancellery to the various prefectures and commanderies.
In the capital, the Army Commanders resisted the edict,
unwilling to implement the regulations.
As the intent of the edict did not permit this,
they were temporarily allowed to request a suspension; within one hundred days, notices were posted to all monasteries
forbidding monks and nuns from leaving.
The Commissioner of Merit for the Left Ward reported:
in accordance with the edict regulating monks and nuns,
excluding those already aged and infirm or whose observance of precepts is precise,
those monks and nuns who clung to their assets and voluntarily returned to secular life numbered one thousand two hundred and thirty-two persons.
The Commissioner of Merit for the Right Ward reported:
in accordance with the edict regulating monks and nuns,
excluding those already aged and infirm or whose observance of precepts is precise,
those monks and nuns who clung to their assets and voluntarily returned to secular life numbered two thousand two hundred and fifty-nine persons.
In response to the report from the Commissioner of Merit for the Right Ward, an imperial edict stated:
According to the edicts of the seventh and
sixteenth days of the tenth month last year,
the regulations ordering the secularization of monks and nuns
should be followed. Regarding those who cling to their assets
and willingly return to secular life,
each is to be entrusted to their native place to be registered as a twice-a-year tax household.
Hereafter, if any circuit has such categories of persons,
they shall all be handled according to this precedent.
As for the slaves and maidservants they keep,
a monk is permitted to retain one,
a nun is permitted to retain two maidservants.
The rest shall each be taken back into custody by their original families.
If they have no family,
the state shall sell them.
Apart from their robes and alms bowls, other assets shall be collected and stored,
awaiting later disposition by edict.
Regarding the slaves and maidservants retained by nuns and monks,
if any possess martial skills or understand various medicines or techniques,
they are not permitted to be retained.
It is not permitted to shave their heads and privately ordain them.
If there are violations,
the monastery administrators and officers shall record and report them to the authorities.
The remaining assets, money, goods, etc.,
shall each be entrusted to the Commissioners of Merit to regulate and report.
First day of the first month, the third year of the Huìchāng era, cyclical year Guǐhài.
On the first day of the second month, an official communique stated:
Monks and nuns who have already returned to secular life
may not arbitrarily enter monasteries or take lodging there.
Furthermore, monks and nuns sent away under guarantee
are not permitted to reside in the capital or enter towns.
The above still pertains to measures triggered by specific events and individuals;
although it involved purification and elimination,
it did not yet constitute a fundamental abolition of Buddhism.
However, when Wéi Zōngqīng's submitted commentary was rejected,
Emperor Wǔzōng's intent to suppress Buddhism had already become clear.
The Pilgrimage Record states:
In the sixth month of the third year of Huìchāng,
the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, Wéi Zōngqīng, composed a twenty-volume commentary on the Nirvana Sutra and presented it.
The present Emperor, having perused it,
burned the sutra commentary,
and issued an edict ordering the Secretariat-Chancellery to go to his residence to seize the drafts and burn them.
The edict text is as follows:

An edict to Wéi Zōngqīng, Grand Master of Silver and Blue Light, Acting Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, Pillar of State, Baron of Guāngyīn County with a fief of three hundred households:
You hold a lofty position among the ranks,
and should adhere to Confucian learning.
Yet you are immersed in heterodox doctrines,
fanning the winds of heresy.
Having opened the path of delusion,
you have completely violated the principles of the classics.
Among the ranks of officials,
how profound is this decay!
Moreover, words that are not sage-like
are still prohibited and rejected;
how can the teachings of foreign lands be allowed to spread?
Although We wish to be tolerant,
We fear it will harm customs and morals.
Demotion to a provincial post
is still considered lenient grace.
You may be appointed Prefect of Chéngdū Prefecture.
Dispatch him by post-horse.
The Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, Wéi Zōngqīng, presented a Buddhist Nirvana Sutra commentary he compiled in three virtues and twenty volumes.
In accordance with the edict, the Great Perfection, Characters of the Yang Mirror Synopsis in twenty volumes
have all been examined in detail.
The Buddha was originally a man of the western barbarians;
his teachings propagate the doctrine of non-birth.
Confucius was a sage of the Central Land;
his classics convey words of benefit.
Yet Wéi Zōngqīng, a scholar long among the Confucian grove,
a member of a distinguished clan of officials,
failed to propagate Confucius and Mozi,
but instead became immersed in belief in Buddhism,
recklessly composing barbarian books,
and lightly presenting them.
Moreover, the common people of China
have long been tainted by this influence.
It is truly fitting to jointly halt this deluding of the deaf,
to make them return to simplicity.
Yet you gathered heretical falsehoods,
further deluding foolish people.
Holding a position in the court ranks,
should you not feel ashamed?
The sutra you presented
has already been burned within the palace.
The draft manuscript is entrusted to the Secretariat-Chancellery to seize and burn,
and it must not be transmitted outside.
The edict was issued on the thirteenth day of the sixth month of the third year of Huìchāng.
The process of suppressing Buddhism,
as seen in the records, is as follows:
In the fourth month of the fifth year of Huìchāng,
it was said that the Commissioner of Merit and Virtue had drafted a proposal regarding the laicization of monks and nuns,
discussing the order of implementation.
First, those under thirty years of age were to be laicized,
followed by those under fifty,
then those over fifty who did not possess a temple registry certificate.
In the third round, those whose temple registry certificates were found to be irregular upon verification were to be laicized.
Finally, even those with temple registry certificates that were not flawed were all to be laicized,
thus completely eliminating monks and nuns.
This plan of action
was uniformly implemented across the realm.
As it was carried out in accordance with the imperial decree,
starting from the first day of the fourth month,
all monks and nuns under thirty years of age were ordered to return to secular life
and sent back to their places of origin.
Three hundred monks were laicized each day.
By the fifteenth day, all monks and nuns under forty had been laicized.
Starting from the sixteenth day,
monks and nuns under fifty were laicized,
and this continued until the tenth day of the fifth month, when it was completed.
Starting from the eleventh day,
those over fifty without temple registry certificates were laicized.
Since the previous year, when the registry of monks and nuns was compiled,
those with coarse conduct who did not adhere to the teachings
were all ordered to return to secular life
and sent back to their places of origin.
This year, no distinction was made between those of high or coarse conduct,
nor was consideration given to the reverence of eminent monks and virtuous ones.
As soon as their turn came,
they were ordered to return to secular life.
Frequent imperial inquiries were made:
How many have already been laicized?
How many have not yet been laicized?
The numbers were urged to be reported.
Foreign monks were not included in the proposal,
and the Commissioner of Merit and Virtue separately memorialized for a decision.
There was a decree stating:
Foreign monks without temple registry certificates
were also to be laicized
and sent back to their own countries.
Nanda from North India in the Western Regions was at Dàxīngshàn Temple.
There was also the Indian Tripitaka Master Bǎoyuè, along with four disciples,
who had completed their studies in Central India,
were skilled in reciting and upholding the great dharma,
and were meticulous in their observance of precepts.
Though well-versed in sutras and treatises and residing at Qīnglóng Temple, they did not possess Táng dynasty temple registry certificates.
Many monks from Silla also lacked temple registry certificates.
The Japanese monks Yuánrén
and Wéizhèng also did not possess Táng dynasty temple registry certificates.
The Commissioner of Merit and Virtue, in accordance with the decree, placed them in the category for laicization.
A notice was also posted to all temples stating:
If any monk or nun refused to comply with laicization,
they would be charged with violating the imperial decree,
and executed on the spot.
An entry from the eighth month states:
Recently, there was a decree
that the black robes of laicized monks and nuns across the realm
were to be collected by their respective prefectures and counties and burned.
It was feared that relatives of officials,
relying on their influence, might hide them in private homes
and secretly wear the black robes.
Therefore, it was necessary to strictly collect and inspect them,
and burn them all, after which a report was to be submitted.
If, after the burning,
any monk or nun was found with black robes not surrendered,
during inspections,
if such items were discovered,
they were to be dealt with according to the decree.
The various prefectures and counties, in accordance with the decree, notified all wards and villages
to collect the robes of monks and nuns,
bring them to the prefectures and counties,
and burn them completely.
There was also a decree ordering that rare treasures, jade ornaments, pearls, gold, and silver from temples across the realm
be collected and inspected by the respective prefectures and counties and submitted to the court.
Another decree stated:
Silver utensils, bells, chimes, cauldrons, and pots used by monks and nuns in temples across the realm
were to be entrusted to the Salt and Iron Commissioners of each circuit for collection into the official treasury,
and a record was to be submitted.
Although the government orders were strict,
in Héběi, due to lax enforcement,
they seemed not to have been fully implemented.
An entry from the eleventh month states:
Over the past three or four years,
prefectures and counties across the realm, in accordance with the decree,
had completely laicized monks and nuns.
Moreover, Buddhist halls, monasteries, and temple buildings across the realm had been completely demolished.
Furthermore, scriptures, images, and monastic robes across the realm had been completely burned.
Additionally, the gold stripped from Buddha statues across the realm had been completed,
and copper and iron Buddhas across the realm had been smashed, weighed, and collected.
Prefectures and counties across the realm had also completed the confiscation of temple funds, properties, estates, and servants and slaves.
Only the four military governors of Zhèn, Yōu, Wèi, and Lù north of the Yellow River,
who had always revered Buddhism,
did not demolish temples,
did not laicize monks and nuns,
and left all matters related to Buddhism
untouched.
Frequent imperial envoys were sent to investigate and punish,
but they said, "If the Son of Heaven himself comes to demolish and burn,
then it shall be done!
But we, your subjects, cannot do such a thing."
Reading this, the specific procedures, scope, and results of Wǔzōng's suppression and eradication of Buddhism
become clearly known,
and indeed, it can supplement the omissions in official histories.
Monks, in addition to swallowing their anger,
also daily spread rumors and slanders
to falsely accuse the emperor and his ministers,
shaking people's hearts.
The Pilgrimage Record contains many such accounts.
For example, regarding Wǔzōng's relationship with Daoist priests, it states:
In the second month of the fourth year of Huìchāng,
the emperor visited Jīnxiān Abbey on the right street,
which was a nunnery.
There was a female Daoist priest in the abbey
of exceptional beauty.
The emperor summoned her and was pleased,
bestowing one thousand bolts of silk by decree,
and then ordered the palace officials to renovate the abbey,
connecting it to the inner palace,
and specially constructing a Jīnxiān Tower.
The abbey was originally dilapidated,
but after renovation, it became splendid and magnificent,
and the emperor frequently visited.
In the eighth month of the fifth year of Huìchāng,
there was a decree banning single-wheeled carts across the realm.
After the order was issued,
anyone found using a single-wheeled cart
was to be executed on the spot.
This was because the emperor believed in Daoist teachings,
and single-wheeled carts would damage the center of the Daoist path,
perhaps fearing it would disturb the Daoist priests' minds!
There was also a decree banning black pigs, black dogs, black donkeys, and black oxen across the realm.
This was because Daoist priests wear yellow,
and perhaps the abundance of black would suppress yellow, causing it to diminish!
An order was also issued for coastal prefectures and counties to present live otters,
though the reason was unknown.
Recently, there was a decree ordering Daoist priests to present the hearts and gallbladders of fifteen-year-old boys and girls,
which was also due to being deceived and misled by Daoist priests.
Regarding Wǔzōng's palace crimes and evils, it states:
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Huìchāng,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
She was Empress Guō of the Tàihé era.
Because the Empress Dowager had a devout heart
and believed in Buddhism,
every time monks and nuns were laicized,
she would remonstrate with words.
The emperor ordered poisoned wine to be presented,
and she was poisoned to death!
Also, Empress Xiāo of the Yìyáng Palace,
who was the current emperor's mother,
was exceptionally beautiful.
The current emperor summoned her to be taken as a consort,
but the Empress Dowager refused to comply.
The emperor took a bow and shot her,
the arrow piercing her chest,
and she died.
Regarding Wǔzōng's improper handling of subordinates, it states:
In the fourth year of Huìchāng, a decree ordered the two armies to build an Immortal Terrace within the palace grounds,
one hundred and fifty feet high.
Starting in the tenth month,
three thousand strong men from the Left and Right Shéncè Armies were used daily
to carry soil and construct it.
The emperor urgently desired its early completion,
and daily decrees urged the construction.
The commanders of the two armies inspected with clubs in hand.
The emperor, while passing by,
asked the eunuch in charge,
"Who are those holding clubs?"
The senior official replied,
"The army commanders are overseeing the terrace construction."
The emperor declared,
"I do not want you overseeing with clubs;
you must carry soil yourselves,"
and thus ordered them to carry soil.
Later, when the emperor again visited the construction site,
he personally took a bow
and, without reason, shot and killed one of the commanders,
an act of extreme tyranny.
Regarding Wǔzōng's death, it is recorded:
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month of the sixth year of Huìchāng,
it was heard that the Son of Heaven had passed away several months earlier.
Throughout the circuits, prefectures, and counties,
mourning and wearing mourning clothes had been completed.
His body had rotted and decayed before he died!
In the fifth month of that year, on the first day,
it records the establishment of Emperor Xuānzōng, stating:
"The new Son of Heaven's surname is Lǐ."
The phrasing is particularly sharp and incisive.
All such accounts
are likely part of the planned propaganda by the monastic community of the time,
not merely the fabrications of Ennin alone.
For at that time, the influence of Buddhism was deeply rooted in people's hearts,
and Emperor Wǔzōng, Lǐ Déyù, and others attempted to resist it with the strength of a few individuals,
thus ultimately meeting with ruin and disgrace.
When Emperor Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
the policy took a complete turn.
Despite Lǐ Déyù's wisdom, tactics, and meritorious achievements,
he fell and never recovered,
largely because he had incurred too many enmities.
As the saying goes, "A red tongue can burn down a city,"
and those who opposed him were not limited to Líng Hú Táo and Cuī Xuàn and their ilk.
(Supplementary Note) Regarding Chinese sources related to the Huìcháng persecution of Buddhism:
The "Old Book of Táng," Annals of Emperor Wǔzōng, records an edict abolishing Buddhism in the eighth month of the fifth year of Huìcháng.
Lǐ Déyù's "Huìcháng Yīpǐn Jí," volume twenty, contains the "Memorial Congratulating the Edict on the Abolition and Destruction of Various Temples."
See also Dù Mù's "Fánchuān Wénjí," volume ten,
the "Record of the Newly Built Nántíngzǐ in Hángzhōu," and the "Táng Huìyào," volume forty-seven,
as well as Sòng Zhào Líndé's "Hóuqīng Lù," volume two,
for reference.
In summary,
although the "Pilgrimage Record" contains erroneous transmissions, mistaken hearsay,
rumors and slanders,
which are pervasive throughout,
due to its antiquity
and the breadth of its scope,
if one can appropriately collate, compare,
discern, and interpret it,
it will certainly benefit those studying Táng history.
In the past, Mr. Liáng Rèngōng, when discussing historical materials,
lamented that the surrounding peoples of our country
were mostly uncivilized,
and their writings that could supplement our historical facts were exceedingly rare.
He regarded the Arab Abū Zayd al-Hasan's "Account of India and China"
and the Italian Marco Polo's travelogue as rare treasures.
In terms of the nature and content of the "Pilgrimage Record,"
it certainly far surpasses these two works.
Dr. Okayoshi Masayuki, in his "History of Japanese Literature in Chinese,"
highly praises Ennin's literary talent,
stating that his writing is not inferior to that of Sugawara no Michizane
or Miyoshi no Kiyoyuki,
that his letters possess the style of Ōuyáng Xiū and Sū Shì's personal notes,
and that his travel accounts are the crown among the five great travelogues.
He also mentions Ennin's skill in waka poetry,
with selections included in the three waka anthologies:
"Shoku Kokin,"
"Shin Kokin,"
and "Shin Shūi."
However, Ennin seems to have devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures,
not pursuing literary embellishment.
During his ten years in Táng,
six of which were spent in Cháng'ān,
he never associated with literati
or immersed himself in elegance.
The "Catalog of Newly Sought Sacred Teachings Brought to Táng"
records the books Ennin brought back,
including many collections of Táng poetry and prose,
yet Ennin's own works
have not been transmitted in either Japan or China.
Compared to Cháo Héng
and Kūkai,
he cannot be mentioned in the same breath.
Upon his return to his homeland,
the Táng monk Qī Bái presented him with a poem, which reads:
"My homeland faces the setting sun,
The sea route trusts the returning oar.
Trees vanish, no shore in sight,
Wind rises, only the tide remains.
The year ends, the journey unfinished,
At sky's edge, the country still far.
Already entered the King of Mín's dream,
Fragrant flowers beckon beyond the border."
(See "Complete Táng Poems")
Ennin, having experienced the vicissitudes of the world,
with mixed sorrow and joy,
and myriad emotions,
left no record of a reply poem.
The "Pilgrimage Record"
is written in a verbose and rambling style,
further marred by errors and omissions,
making it difficult to read through.
Although the work has been transmitted,
it was not printed for a long time.
Entering the Sòng imperial library,
it elicited no response whatsoever,
likely for this very reason.
Occasionally, there are noteworthy passages,
such as in volume three, which describes the scenery of Wǔtái Mountain:
"Zhōngtái is the center of the four peaks.
Throughout the peak, water gushes forth, and the ground is soft.
The grass grows over an inch long,
lush and dense,
covering the ground as it grows.
When stepped on, it flattens,
but springs back when the foot is lifted.
With each step, the ground is wet,
cold as ice.
Everywhere there are small depressions,
all filled with water!
Across the peak, sand and stones are intermingled,
with countless stone pagodas.
Delicate, soft grass
grows among moss and lichen.
Although the ground is wet,
there is no muddy sludge,
because the moss and soft grass
have densely spread their roots,
thus preventing travelers from dirtying their shoes and feet.
Strange flowers of extraordinary colors
bloom all over the mountain.
Upon leisurely reaching the summit,
flowers are seen on all sides,
as if brocade were spread out.
Their delicate fragrance
perfumes one's clothing.
People say that even now, in the fifth month, it is still cold,
and the flowers are not yet in full bloom.
In the sixth
and seventh months,
the flowers are said to bloom even more profusely.
Looking at the colors of these flowers,
they are unlike any found in the human world."
It also records the origin of the equal offerings to monks and laypeople in the mountains, stating:
"Those who enter this mountain (Wǔtái Mountain)
naturally develop a mind of equality.
When meals are provided in the mountain,
regardless of whether one is monk or layperson, male or female, young or old,
offerings are made equally.
Without regard to status or age,
all are regarded as manifestations of Mañjuśrī.
In the past, during a grand feast at the Great Huáyán Temple,
all common men and women, beggars, and the poor came to receive offerings.
The donor complained, saying:
'Having traveled far over mountains and slopes
to make offerings here,
my intention was solely to provide for the monks in the mountain.
Yet these worldly beggars
all come to receive food.
If we are to feed such beggars,
we might as well hold the feast locally.
What need is there to come all the way to this mountain?'
The monks urged that all be given food.
Among the beggars was a pregnant woman,
who, seated with child,
received her portion of food.
She then asked for a portion for the child in her womb.
The donor scolded her
and refused to give it.
The pregnant woman repeatedly said:
'The child in my womb,
though not yet born,
is also a person.
Why not give it food?'
The donor replied:
'You are foolish!
Though the child in your belly counts as one,
it has not come out.
If given food,
who would eat it?'
The woman responded:
'If the child in my belly does not receive food,
then I too should not eat.'
She then rose and left the dining hall.
As soon as she passed through the hall's door,
she transformed into Mañjuśrī,
radiating light that illuminated
the entire hall brilliantly.
With a countenance like pure jade,
riding a golden-maned lion,
surrounded by ten thousand Buddhas,
she soared into the sky and departed.
The entire assembly,
numbering in the thousands,
rushed out all at once,
bewildered and falling to the ground unconsciously.
They raised their voices in repentance and apology,
weeping tears like rain,
and together chanted the name of the great sage Mañjuśrī.
Until their voices were exhausted and throats parched,
they received no glance in return.
She vanished as if an illusion!
The great assembly
could not taste their meal.
Each made a vow:
From that day forward,
when making offerings or holding feasts,
regardless of gender, age, status, wealth, or poverty,
all must be provided for equally.
The custom of the mountain
thus established the rule of equality."
Such accounts,
whether describing extraordinary scenery
or recounting whimsical tales,
require no deliberate embellishment
to become masterpieces of refined literature.
Rather than attributing their lasting value to Rénzhī's literary skill,
it would be more accurate to say that his profound immersion in ancient texts,
his reverence for renowned mountains,
and the majestic landscapes within his mind are truly unparalleled!
Japanese students sent to study in the Tang dynasty,
including scholar-monks,
all received generous hospitality from the Chinese court and society,
with care and protection
extending to the smallest details.
Eminent monks and great virtues,
embodying the spirit of universal compassion,
promoted the ancient teaching of educating all without discrimination.
Those who sought instruction and guidance
all departed having obtained what they desired.
Thus, figures like Saichō
and Kūkai,
grateful to their teachers,
remembered them for the rest of their lives,
yearning for the Central Plains
as if it were a heavenly realm.
Ennin achieved fame at a young age,
his reputation widely celebrated,
and by the time he passed forty,
he had nurtured many disciples.
Surviving countless perils,
he braved the seas to journey eastward,
his fervor for seeking the Dharma
no less than that of his predecessors.
Yet, when he sought an audience at Tiāntái, he was obstructed;
when he stayed in Hǎizhōu, he was expelled;
hiding along the island shores,
he relied on connections with influential figures
to finally fulfill his long-held wish of paying homage at Wǔtái
and studying in Cháng'ān.
Soon after, he encountered the calamity of the Huìchāng persecution of Buddhism,
forcing him to grow his hair and change his attire,
his heart filled with sorrow and frustration.
Witnessing the spread of rumors and slander,
the estrangement between ruler and people,
and the bizarre and erratic government decrees,
he found it impossible to seek clarity.
Before even leaving the country,
he heard that the policies against Buddhism
had already been reversed,
with orders changing from morning to evening,
utterly undermining authority and trust.
Indeed, after Ennin and others returned,
Japan ceased sending envoys to the Tang dynasty,
and the Tang itself began its decline from then on!
When the Duke of Zhōu cultivated virtue, the Yuècháng clan came to pay tribute.
The leadership of culture—
how easily can it be spoken of!
